title: A branch knows which spec it owes
evidence: The author reports the inference is wrong about half the time (2026-08-06 notes). merge-ready grades the spec it infers, so a wrong inference grades the wrong contract -- and with three branches in flight under an orchestrator, the wrong one is likely to be another live branch's rather than nothing. Prior art: spec-and-read-verbs-scope (done) narrowed inference to where a spec is used and named the near miss, and no-store-inference-on-main (done) stopped main inferring from the store, so this is the third pass and the remaining error should be characterised before it is fixed. merge-ready already prefers a spec the branch owes over a plan it merely wrote and names which it graded and how it got there, so the report exists; what is missing is the inference being right.

title: A spec whose file is present but whose Deliverable/Proof section becomes unparseable (bad merge, stray conflict markers, a mangled heading) while it is genuinely owed and untouched by any branch reads as "authored as plan" and is silently exempted from the spec and clauses legs
deliverable: Either specClausesDiffer/clauseIdsDiffer treats a clause count that dropped to zero on head (versus a nonzero base) as something other than ordinary authorship — e.g. unmet/unknown rather than a plan — or doctor's specIssues gains a check that a spec's parsed clause count did not collapse relative to its own recorded audit-pass clause ids while members remain open, so a corrupted-but-present spec fails loud instead of exempting the branch that broke it
evidence: Reproduced directly against the exported functions with a temp git repository: committed a-spec.md with two tagged clauses on main, then on a feature branch overwrote the same path with unresolved merge-conflict markers and no parseable "## Deliverable" section (the file still exists, so existsSync-based checks pass). specClausesDiffer(config, 'main', headSha, 'a-spec') returned true (0 parsed clauses on head versus 2 on base), and authoredAsPlan([{state:'open'}], true) returned true — the spec reads as an authored plan and merge-ready's spec/clauses legs are skipped with "No other spec was graded." doctor's specIssues(config) on the same tree returned an empty array: it only reports duplicate clause ids or an unreadable file, neither of which fires here, so nothing else in the merge gate catches it. This is exactly the "spec file that does not parse" seam the spec's own decisions call for a defensible verdict on, and the verdict produced is the accidental exemption the spec explicitly says must not happen. Outright deletion of the same file is caught separately, because checkStore's specExists(existsSync) check fails doctor with an error in that case — corruption-without-deletion is the gap.

title: touchedWriteRegion (decideSpec's c7 discriminator) trusts a task's declared `writes` grant as a stand-in for "this branch's diff did work against the spec," but the repository's own workflow (workPrompt.ts) documents that a diff diverging from its declared writes later is sanctioned, not a violation — so a spec with a stale or incomplete grant can be dropped as a candidate and merge-ready passes with no spec graded even though real, undeclared work landed
deliverable: touchedWriteRegion needs a signal beyond the stored writes grant before it drops a spec — for example, falling back to "touched" whenever this branch is the one that most recently wrote store events against the spec and has any commits at all (matching the existing fail-open polarity used when git cannot answer), or adding a doctor/merge-ready check that flags a branch whose diff falls outside every open task's declared writes for its own active spec as a stale-grant warning rather than staying silent
evidence: Reproduced directly with a temp git repository and the exported changedFiles/diffTouchesRegion functions, mirroring branchStanding's own region construction (specFile(spec) plus membersOf(spec).flatMap(task => task.writes)): committed a-spec.md and scripts/other-decl.ts on main (the latter standing in for the task's declared writes grant), then on a feature branch committed real work at scripts/actual-file.ts instead — a path the grant never named, and the spec file itself was never touched, which is the ordinary case since most implementation work does not hand-edit the spec markdown. changedFiles reported only scripts/actual-file.ts, and diffTouchesRegion(changed, ['specs/a-spec.md', 'scripts/other-decl.ts']) returned false. In decideSpec this spec is filtered out of `touched` before it can ever be graded, so if it were the branch's only candidate the gate reports "this branch is working no spec, so it owes no clause" over real, unaudited work. This branch's own task record needed exactly this kind of grant correction mid-flight (commit b31f0d5, "Correct the write grant"), so drift between a declared grant and the real diff is not a hypothetical here.

title: A brand-new, not-yet-populated spec reads as owed rather than as the plan it is
deliverable:
Either accept that a not-yet-populated spec is graded as owed and record that the choice was
deliberate, since it currently reads as coincidental, or give specClausesDiffer a way to read "absent from
base and still empty on head" as differing the same way "absent from base and now populated" already
does, so a freshly scaffolded plan is not asked to pass an audit over zero clauses before it can be
recognised as a plan.
evidence:
specClausesDiffer compares an absent-from-base clause set, empty, against a head clause set that
also happens to be empty when a spec file has been freshly created but not yet populated with a Proof
list. clauseIdsDiffer([], []) reads two empty sets as identical, so clausesDiffer is false, and
authoredAsPlan requires clausesDiffer===true to grant the plan exemption — so an all-open,
freshly-scaffolded, not-yet-authored spec is graded as a contract this branch owes rather than as the plan
it plainly is, and merge-ready's clauses leg then fails demanding an audit pass over a document with
nothing in it yet. Verified directly by calling clauseIdsDiffer([], []) (returns false) and
authoredAsPlan(open-members, false) (returns false) through the repository's own module resolution. This
is on the safe side pass 1 asked to be favoured — it blocks rather than waves through — so I am filing it
as non-blocking, but it is a real, reachable misclassification: a spec entering `written`
(specsWrittenFromBranch) before its Proof list is authored, for example immediately after a member is
scaffolded against the spec but before the spec doc itself is filled in, hits exactly this path.
reason: Accepted as deliberate, not a defect. A spec absent from base and still empty on head has no clause id for head to lack, so headAddsClauseId reads it as owed rather than as a plan -- the coordinator's ruling on finding 1 (grade the plan exemption on whether head adds an id, not on a symmetric difference) explicitly disposes of this: pure absence of content is not evidence of authorship any more than pure deletion is, and erring toward grading (demanding an audit) is the safe direction the spec asks for. A freshly-scaffolded, not-yet-authored spec earns its plan exemption once a real clause is written, which is the same trigger that already exempts any other brand-new spec.

title: Pass 1's finding 1 is only closed for total corruption, not partial
deliverable:
specClausesDiffer's corruption guard, the headClauses.length===0 and baseClauses.length>0
check, needs to catch partial clause loss from a mangled document, not only total loss, so a spec that is
genuinely owed and untouched but happened to get corrupted by a bad merge cannot exempt itself from the
gate by losing only some of its clauses instead of all of them. One direction: also refuse the exemption
whenever the deliverable section shows signs of not having been intentionally authored, such as a missing
Proof marker, literal merge-conflict-marker text inside the section, or a clause id present in the last
recorded audit pass's verdicts that silently vanished from the head parse with no new id replacing it.
evidence:
specClausesDiffer refuses the plan exemption only when the head copy parses to exactly zero clauses
against a populated base. A merge or rebase that leaves stray conflict-marker text over one bullet in the
middle of a Proof list, one of the three corruption causes pass 1's own finding named, drops that one
clause from the scan while leaving the rest intact, so headClauses.length is nonzero and the guard never
fires. The id-set comparison then reads the reduced set as differing from base, indistinguishable from an
intentional edit, and if every member is still open the spec reads as an authored plan again. Reproduced
directly with a temporary git repository against the exported branchStanding and specClausesDiffer
functions: base commit has a-spec.md with three tagged clauses (c1, c2, c3) and one open member whose
writes grant includes impl.ts; the feature-branch commit overwrites the middle bullet's line with literal
conflict-marker text while leaving the Deliverable heading, the Proof marker, and the other two bullets
intact. specClausesDiffer(config, main, resolveCommit(main), a-spec) returns true rather than null, and
branchStanding(config, main) reports spec a-spec, specAuthoredHere true. Before this whole branch existed,
the old file-existence check could not have produced this outcome for a file that already existed on
base, corrupted or not, because it never looked at clause content at all — this is a new failure mode this
branch's clause-identity approach introduced, of which pass 1 caught only the boundary case. doctor's
specIssues does not catch it either; it only flags duplicate clause ids or an unreadable file. I believe
this branch should not merge without addressing this: it is the same defect class pass 1 filed as HIGH,
reopened through a narrower door the fix did not anticipate.

title: A clause can be deferred, and a spec can carry its goal
evidence: A clause stands met, unmet or unknown. There is no way to say a branch deliberately dropped one, so the honest moves are to leave it outstanding -- which blocks merge-ready's spec leg forever -- or to edit the spec, which rewrites the contract silently and leaves the audit grading something nobody promised. Measured in this planning session: adding c8 to reimplement-localization shifted every clause after it and required rewiring --discharges across three task records by hand, with nothing checking the result; a fumble there would have left a clause owed by nobody and merge-ready would have passed a branch that dropped scope. The task-goal half comes from the author's notes (2026-08-06): task growth is recurring and usually not scope drift, because knowledge grows once a worker finishes its first round, and there is often a gap between a spec's clauses and the spirit of the task -- the audit-prompt-brief task had specific clauses while the actual goal was to settle the audit prompt, which nobody could have foreseen when writing it. Auditors already make evidence-based value judgements, so a recorded goal gives them something to judge against. Both halves are one problem: a contract written before the knowledge exists needs an honest way to record what was learned.

title: A deliverable understood better after implementation can only be changed by splitting the branch
deliverable: tasks spec amend copies the current Deliverable verbatim into an Amendments section with a date and a reason, lets the new text stand, and the gate compares against the last amendment. Changing a deliverable stays loud and stays in git, without splitting the branch.
evidence: The Deliverable section freezes when the branch opens and the only sanctioned change is closing the spec and opening another. There is no recorded-amendment path, so a requirement learned during implementation has nowhere to go except unfrozen prose or a branch split. Clause 2 was in fact reinterpreted in the unfrozen Decisions section one commit before the audit that graded it.

title: a note or title cannot begin with two dashes, because the parser has no end-of-flags separator
deliverable: a positional argument beginning with -- is recordable, by the conventional end-of-flags separator
evidence: Found by U7 while writing a real decision event: tasks decision "--actor is named by each writing command" is parsed as an unknown flag and refused. Pre-existing in U6's arity-aware parser rather than introduced by it — tasks add "--x" has the same shape. The conventional fix is an end-of-flags -- separator, which means touching the parser U7 was told to reuse rather than fork, so it was left alone and the decision reworded. Low: it costs a rephrase, and the refusal is loud rather than silent, which is the polarity c2 asks for.

title: a record cannot be removed, and a grant cannot be cleared
deliverable: Give the store a route to retract a record that should never have been one, and let tasks edit clear an optional field. Either a delete verb for a declined record nothing references, or accept an empty --grant the way --discharges and --requires already accept one. Both routes exist for other fields; grant is the outlier that refuses the empty value, and there is no route at all for a whole record.
evidence: 2026-08-06: cleaning three scratch probes (scratch-ruling-probe, c11-proof-probe, orch-verify-probe), declined 2026-08-05 as 'not real work', each declaring a forecast grant over an empty writes list so doctor warns on all three. tasks edit --grant '' returns 'must be one of forecast, commitment', and no delete verb exists, so the only route was hand-editing docs/tasks.jsonl -- the one file the system exists to keep agents out of, and the file the-task-store-survives-parallel-branches is about to make sort-canonical.

title: A recorded audit pass is never checked against the diff being merged
deliverable: check --merge refuses when the latest pass head is not an ancestor of HEAD, naming how many commits have landed since the audit.
evidence: cmdAudit computes base and head from git specifically to pin the reviewed range; checkMergeGate reads only verdicts and pass number. Audit once, then land any amount of unaudited code, and the gate stays green. Rule 2 says the audit reads a diff; nothing verifies which diff.

title: A worker can call its spec defective, at two levels
deliverable: Give kind 'question' its behaviour as the worker-to-planner channel, at two levels. Level 1 records against the spec and clause without blocking, and must reach the auditor's brief so a clause reinterpreted mid-branch is not graded as written. Level 2 additionally names itself in the spec members' requires, which halts dispatch through machinery that already works. Decide the verb and whether severity or an explicit flag separates the levels; naming is a planning decision, not a worker's.
evidence: Author's request 2026-08-06. A worker has no channel back to the spec. tasks note --spec records prose that nothing routes, nothing distinguishes 'FYI' from 'I am blocked', and nothing stops a dispatch. Two levels are wanted: (1) the spec is wrong but the fix is obvious, so the worker records it and continues -- what happened on the-task-store-survives-parallel-branches c2, where the clause enumerated four sites and the rule covered six, handled by hand over one SendMessage and a decision note; (2) the spec does not make sense and there is no obvious course, so the whole spec goes back to the author plus a planning agent and the work stops. THE MACHINERY LARGELY EXISTS AND IS DEAD. Kind 'question' is in the Kind union, in KINDS, accepted by tasks add at records.ts:103, and used by ZERO records - a declared noun with no behaviour. And level 2's blocking needs nothing new: isBlocked is waitingOn().length > 0, and requirementStates releases on BOTH done and declined, so filing a question record and naming it in the members' requires makes tasks next skip them, work-prompt refuse, and roadmap show them blocked - with answering it (done) or dismissing it (declined) unblocking automatically. Level 1 is the same record without the requires edges. Distinct from clause deferral: a deferral says the WORK fell short but the goal is served, recorded by the auditor at audit time; a defect says the CONTRACT is wrong, recorded by the worker at work time. They share surfaces but must not merge.
reason: Superseded by the-workflow-records-what-cost-it-in-one-place-with-o, which is the same system rather than two. These were the write half (a worker calls its spec defective, at two levels) and the read half (a planner counts defects by class), filed hours apart, and the author's observation is that tool friction is the same shape as both -- an event that cost a round, logged so a future session can plan against it. Keeping them separate would have produced two channels a worker chooses between at the moment it is least able to classify, and two queries a planner has to remember to run. Every finding in their evidence survives in the successor: the dead kind 'question', blocking for free via isBlocked and requires, the decision and spec-* op precedents, and the denominator point. What the merge adds is the second axis -- fault -- and the rule that an unknowable question must not count as a defect.

title: a patch that adds type: to an existing entity inherits nothing, silently
deliverable: The template base applies whenever type: first appears on an entity, whichever module writes it — or a patch introducing type: is refused with a message saying why.
evidence: entityTypeBase is reached through byId.get(id)?.value ?? entityTypeBase(...), so it is consulted only on an entity's FIRST declaration. Reproduced: base module declares '# entitytype melee-foe' and '# entity rat' with no type; a patch module declares '# entity base.rat' + 'type: base.melee-foe'. Result: rat.type='base.melee-foe', rat.actions=[]. The type: resolves, validates, survives pruning and serializes; nothing errors. Patch-a-section-into-existence is the DSL's headline merge rule (merge.ts:80-83) and type: is the one field that silently opts out.

title: # recipe cadence is unvalidated, so a recipe compiles the action the grammar refuses
deliverable: recipeSchema validates time:/rate: positivity at load, with the action grammar's message.
evidence: rate: { parser: numberOrStat } has no positivity check and spannable only tests rate !== undefined. Reproduced: '# recipe dig / rate: 0' loads clean, compiles {kind:'continuous',rate:0}, and the first craft throws 'impossible attempt duration (Infinity)'; rate: -30 gives (-2000); time: -3 silently compiles to an instant craft. rate: 0 authored on an action is a load error. rate: on recipes is new in this branch.

title: serialize prints a template-bearing entity in a form that will not reload
deliverable: entitySection prints only what the entity authored over its template, so print-then-load is a fixpoint for a template-bearing entity.
evidence: entitySection prints type: AND the fully flattened action list, so a reload merges the entity onto the template a second time. Reproduced end to end: entity overriding a 'continuous / rate: 30' template action with 'instant' prints 'fight:/instant/rate: 30' and the reload fails with 'an instant action takes no rate:'. Reaches two real workflows: scripts/squash-local-changes.ts:116 serialize-then-reloads and hard-fails, and src/content/modportal.ts:153 canonicalises every web contribution the same way. Even in the benign case the printer restates all ~14 inherited lines on the shipped rat, so a later edit to the template no longer reaches the canonicalised entity; registryDiff is 0, which is why the round-trip gate misses it.

title: the kind/cadence table is enforced on the authored block only, so merge assembles actions the loader refuses
deliverable: The kind/cadence table runs over each merged action at build time, so an unauthorable action cannot be assembled by merge.
evidence: resolveKind runs inside actionBody.parseBlock; nothing re-checks after mergeEntries/overlay. Reproduced: template 'fight: continuous / rate: swing-rate' with entity block 'fight: time: 5' merges to {kind:'continuous',time:5,rate:'swing-rate'} and attemptDuration returns 2000ms — the authored time: 5 is discarded with no diagnostic; the same pair authored directly is 'action time: and rate: are the same axis'. Second case: template 'continuous / rate: 30' with entity 'fight: instant' merges to {kind:'instant',rate:30}, which authored directly is 'an instant action takes no rate:'. Templates make these reachable but a plain cross-module entity patch reaches them too.

title: grammar.md, which AGENTS.md calls authoritative, now teaches action syntax that fails to load
deliverable: grammar.md's action section documents instant/duration/continuous, rate:, default-action-duration, # entitytype and type: — or the file loses its authoritative designation.
evidence: AGENTS.md:20 points readers at docs/dsl-rewrite/grammar.md for the authoritative grammar. It still documents repeating as a bare tag (:249, :262-264, :423), speed: <stat-id> as a field (:529), time: as 'defaults to 0 (instant) if omitted' (:524-525), and carries a worked repeating + speed: cooking-speed example (:579-580). After this branch speed: is a hard load error and repeating is a silently ignored no-op. The section was correct before the branch, so it is strictly worse now.

title: the unknown-entitytype message has two hand-duplicated producers
deliverable: One owner for the message, so drift in either producer is visible.
evidence: src/content/registry.ts:301 emits it from the merge path and the put(section,'type','entitytype',...) site in referenceSites.ts:195 emits it from post-build validation. entityType.test.ts:118 and :135 hit the two different producers with one regex each, so either can drift without a test noticing.

title: three references.test.ts cases inject the retired word repeating into their fixture

evidence: src/content/references.test.ts:152-153 and :159-161 call loading('  continuous', '  repeating\n  requires: ...'), replacing the continuous tag with repeating — now a silently-ignored unknown bare tag. strike becomes an untagged cadence-less action rather than the continuous one it is meant to be; the assertions still pass because they check an unrelated error.

title: time: with a non-numeric value lost its field-named parse error
deliverable: A non-numeric cadence reports a message naming the field, with the line's span.
evidence: Measured both sides: on main '# entity clock / tick: / time: abc' reports 'action time requires a non-negative number'; on this branch it reports 'expected a number'. The seconds parser delegates to decimal.parse, whose generic message has no field context and builds a zero-width span at the cursor instead of using line.span.

title: two runtime cadence errors still tell authors to fix speed:
deliverable: Both messages name rate: instead of the retired speed:.
evidence: src/runtime/runtime.ts:152 and :227 both end 'give it a positive time: or a positive speed stat'. The sibling guard at :421 was reworded in b93f18d; these two were missed, and speed: is now a load error so the advice cannot be followed.

title: the mod portal hand-maintains its own section-kind list, and a new kind was added to the loader without it
deliverable: The rename set is derived from the declared partition, so a kind added to the loader cannot be forgotten in the portal.
evidence: canonicalLocalChangesModule listed 11 kind/map pairs by hand; this branch added entitytype to SCHEMAS, CONTENT_SECTION_MAPS, NAMESPACED_KINDS, ReferenceKind and visitSection and missed it. Reproduced end to end: a contribution declaring '# entitytype foe' and '# entity rat / type: foe' canonicalises to a module with no # entitytype section (its id was never renamed, so serialize's own-module filter dropped it) while the entity's type: WAS renamed to point at it — the published mod then fails with '# entity approved-mod-7.rat type: names an unknown entitytype: approved-mod-7.foe', blaming the contributor. Same shape as the contribution system's open 2026-07-30 H1.

title: the spec's Decisions block contradicted the shipped code on action tags
deliverable: The Decisions block records the reversal and the inputs that stop loading because of it.
evidence: The block recorded 'an unknown bare tag on an action stays silently ignored' as settled. The promoted 'once' work reversed that and the record was never corrected — and a spec becomes the historical record on merge (docs/workflow.md:6-8). Three inputs that loaded on main now fail and none was named: any unread bare tag on an action, a duration clause on an action, and '# recipe / time: 0'.

title: Action labels as namespace members
evidence: The one piece of DSL-modules chunk 3c deferred. Flags and dialogue nodes are paths in the namespace tree; action labels are not. Nothing is broken today — labels are validated in src/content/references.ts and their objId is already namespaced — so this buys uniformity, not a fix. Needs a slug/display split (labels carry spaces: "pick lock") and rewrites the use:<kind>.<objId>.<label> choice-id contract in src/runtime/session.ts and src/content/test.ts. Do it with the GUI rebuild, which redefines that contract anyway, rather than churning it twice.

title: Give actions a named kind (instant/duration/continuous) instead of overloading time:
evidence: SETTLED 2026-07-29. time: is seconds per attempt and the kind is what ends the action — orthogonal axes today conflated into one field ("time: 60" as folklore for "speed: reads as per-minute"). Each kind carries exactly one cadence field: instant (bare tag, no cadence fields), duration (untagged default, time: optional via # variable default-action-duration), continuous (bare tag renaming repeating, rate: required, time:/speed: rejected). rate: accepts a literal (per minute) or a stat id. Four load errors enforce the table. Closes TODO(default-duration) (action.ts:19) and the combat log's F2. Prerequisite: tag the genuinely-instant actions (mirror, stairs, eat) instant before raising default-action-duration above 0, or they become spannable. Shipped surface is small: 5 time: lines, 1 repeating.

title: Amending a clause orphans its undelivered task
deliverable: A proof clause carries an identity that survives both rewording and reordering, so an undelivered task stays bound to its clause across an amendment. Either spec amend repoints existing undelivered tasks as part of the amendment, or clauses get a stable id that verdicts and task ids reference instead of text or position.
evidence: cmdDone matches an undelivered task's stored deliverable against the spec's current proof clauses to find its verdict. spec amend rewrites clause text, so the task is orphaned and refuses to close: task-system-v2-clause-1 is undelivered but its clause text no longer matches any proof clause. Hit for real while closing clause 1 on this branch; the workaround was tasks edit to repoint it by hand. Matching by ordinal index instead has the mirror-image defect the pass-1 audit already noted - inserting a clause silently rebinds every recorded verdict and every slug-clause-N id.

title: an extra positional argument is silently discarded, which is c9's promise broken through the door c9 did not name
deliverable: a positional argument a command does not use is an error naming it, exactly as an unrecognised flag is
evidence: Found by dogfooding on 2026-08-02, by the orchestrator making the mistake. 'tasks note <id> --actor X "<text>"' recorded the id as the note text and discarded the text, because note's signature is note "<text>" [--id <id>]. Reproduced deliberately: 'tasks note "first" "second" "third"' records only first, and 'tasks add "a title" "an extra positional"' takes the title and drops the rest. Both exit 0. c9 promises no command answers a question it did not understand and none silently discards one it did; U6 implemented that for flag NAMES and U4 for flag VALUES, and positionals were named in neither. The consequence is the founding defect's shape exactly — a confident wrong answer with no signal — and here it cost a recorded note that a reader would never know was missing. Worth noting what did work: the tool disclosed 'recorded a note against no system/no spec', and I did not read it. A quieter tool would have said nothing at all.

title: Three archetype mods: assassin, berserker, thorns
deliverable: Item bases and a mod pack per archetype, authored in the DSL rather than coded. Each is a different shape of the same primitives - poison is a damage-over-time debuff on hit, rage is a resource with a constant drain that grants a stat bonus per point held, accelerated vigor is a chance-gated stacking buff granting a percent bonus per stack, thorns is a persistent effect on damage-taken - so authoring them all is the test that the engine generalized rather than growing special cases. Rage and accelerated vigor are deliberately both present: a resource has a ceiling and a rate that regeneration can push against, a stack count has neither, and between them they exercise both counter sources of the one per-counter modifier shape. Doubles as the first real exercise of the contribution/mod path.

title: A refused mutate run leaves its journal on disk, and the next run in that tree silently reverts committed source to it
deliverable: `main()` clears the journal on the refusal path the way the success path does at scripts/mutate.ts:700, and `recoverFrom` refuses to write bytes captured at a commit the tree is no longer on — a journal that records the HEAD it captured from, and reports rather than restores when they differ, turns a silent revert into a message. Until then the brief's own artifact arms the trap on every audit, because c3 makes a refusal the guaranteed first outcome of the manifest it generates.
evidence:
Reproduced twice this session in a clean tree, with real loss of committed work both times. The first `npm run mutate` of this pass printed `recovered 2 file(s) left mutated by an interrupted run: scripts/tasks/audit.ts, scripts/lib/specDoc.ts` and then refused on a find miss; `git status` went from clean to `M scripts/lib/specDoc.ts`, `M scripts/tasks/audit.ts` and `git diff --stat` showed 89 lines gone from audit.ts and 5 from specDoc.ts — exactly commit 8cbd399, reverted, by a run that mutated nothing. `git checkout` restored it, the next invocation reverted it again, and only `rm %TEMP%\universalis-mutate-8b3f33cadc7e3ee9.json` broke the loop.
Mechanism: mutate.ts:615-636 writes the journal as a lock and fills it with the captured bytes before any refusal is computed; the refusal exit at mutate.ts:664-668 does `console.log(...); process.exit(1)` with no `rmSync(JOURNAL)`, unlike the success path at :700. The next run sees a journal whose pid is dead, `journalVerdict` returns `recover`, and `recoverFrom` writes every entry whose current content differs — with no check that the tree is at the commit those bytes came from. `scripts/mutate.ts` is outside this branch's diff, but this branch is what makes the refusal path universal: every entry the brief generates ships the UNRETARGETED sentinel, so the first `npm run mutate` of every audit is refused by construction and leaves a journal behind.
Re-run: run `npm run mutate` on a generated manifest (refused, leaves the journal), commit or edit any file the manifest names, then run mutate again and diff the tree.

title: audit-prompt silently overwrites the aimed manifest and the filled-in pass file it told the auditor to work in
deliverable: Write each artifact only when it is absent, or write to a fresh path per run and name it, so re-reading the brief cannot destroy a pass's evidence. Whichever is chosen, the brief should say which file is the auditor's working copy.
evidence: Both artifacts go to paths derived from slug and pass number alone and both `writeFileSync` unconditionally, while the procedure tells the auditor to aim %TEMP%\mutations-<slug>.json at step 4 and to fill in %TEMP%\audit-<slug>-pass<N>.txt at step 7. The brief is 266 lines and is the auditor's only starting position, so re-running `audit-prompt` mid-audit is the ordinary way to re-read it, and it discards an aimed manifest and a part-written pass with no warning and no backup. All three recorded passes worked on a copy of the manifest; nothing in the brief says to.

title: c8's pass-file proof target passes off a file earlier suite runs left in the shared OS temp directory
deliverable: Make the directory the brief writes its two artifacts into injectable, a config field or an env var the fixture sets, so the test asserts against a path its own fixture owns and `npm test` stops writing into the developer's real temp directory. Then re-run the mutation below and require it to be KILLED.
evidence: Delete audit.ts:651, the `writeFileSync(argsPath, auditArgsSkeleton(...))`, and "writes the pass file the auditor fills in, rather than describing its format" SURVIVED, escalating all the way to whole-suite scope, 0 failed of 1613. It survives because the test reads the absolute path out of stdout and `readFileSync`s it, and %TEMP%\audit-demo-spec-pass1.txt and audit-demo-spec-pass2.txt are sitting there from earlier suite runs on this machine, timestamps 09:23 and 09:24, before this pass started. So the clause's headline behaviour, that the last artifact the procedure names is written rather than described, has no guard, and the same fixed-path write means every `npm test` run drops files into the real OS temp dir. Every other temp-writing test in the repo takes `mkdtempSync` instead; audit.ts:591 and :650 are the only fixed shared-tmp paths in scripts/.

title: c9's "not every spec in the checkout" target admits the exact regression it names
deliverable: Assert the number of slugs the line lists, or that a named third spec is absent from it, instead of counting occurrences of the substring "spec" in a line that also carries the specs directory path. The cap at audit.ts:702 should not be removable with a green suite.
evidence: Replace `otherSpecs.slice(0, 2)` with `otherSpecs` at audit.ts:702, printing every spec in the checkout, which is the behaviour the clause exists to exclude, and "names one other spec to check the standing against, not every spec in the checkout" SURVIVED, escalating to whole-suite scope, 0 failed of 1613. The fixture writes three extra specs and the guard is `expect(line.match(/spec/g).length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(4)`; with all three listed the count is three slugs plus the specs directory in the `ls` hint, exactly 4, so the bound passes. The behaviour in the code is correct; nothing holds it there.

title: parseSpecDoc computes deliverableProse and decisionsSection for no reader
deliverable: Delete both fields and the comment above them. `deliverableSection` is what specCmds.ts reads and what the clause parser splits; nothing else needs a second slice of the same text.
evidence: Both were added in 8cbd399 so the brief could print the spec's prose and decisions; 1ed1c19 removed that printing under the c9 decision "the brief prints no prose it did not compute", and the fields stayed. Grepping the repo for either name finds only their own declaration and assignment, no consumer and no test. They are not free: `deliverableProse` is the first candidate the generated manifest offers for every c3-c6 entry, and aiming c3's entry with it SURVIVED whole-suite scope, because deleting a field nothing reads cannot fail anything.

title: The procedure hands over a pass file and the command to file it on a slug it has just warned twice is not this branch's, while the manifest beside it is suppressed for that reason
deliverable: Gate the skeleton write and the wording of steps 4 and 7 on the same `rangeIsThisSlugs` fact the manifest already reads, so a foreign-slug brief says why it is not offering a pass file rather than naming one and printing the command that records it.
evidence: `npm run tasks -- audit-prompt tasks-roadmap` on this branch prints both WARNINGs, and `writeMutationManifest` correctly refuses: "No mutation manifest: the diff above is not tasks-roadmap's, so every line it could break belongs to work these clauses do not describe." Step 4 then says "Aim the manifest named under `Mutation manifest:` below", there is none, and step 7 writes %TEMP%\audit-tasks-roadmap-pass3.txt and prints `npm run tasks -- audit tasks-roadmap --args-from <it>`. Following it appends a pass 3 to a merged spec's `## Audit passes` and creates undelivered tasks in docs/tasks.jsonl, so this half writes tracked repo state where the guarded half only wasted time. Verified live at 09:27; the file was written and removed by hand afterwards.

title: `mutate` decides a journal is restorable from HEAD alone, so a journal left at the same commit weeks ago is still written over the working tree
deliverable: `recoveryStanding` takes the journal's age as well as its commit and reports rather than restores past the same bound `journalVerdict` already uses, so the two staleness questions are answered from one threshold instead of one being answered and the other left open.
evidence: `recoveryStanding` reads only `journal.head` against `headOf(repoRoot)`. A journal whose pid is dead and whose commit matches is recovered at any age: `journalVerdict`'s six-hour `STALE_AFTER_MS` decides busy-vs-recover for a *live* pid and plays no part here. The spec's own decision says "they might be a month old; nothing in the journal distinguishes those" — but `startedAt` is in the journal, is parsed by `readJournal`, and is already the repo's notion of a run too old to be running. So the one field that answers the age question is present and unread, and the failure it leaves is the same one this clause exists to close: uncommitted work at an unchanged HEAD silently reverted to bytes some earlier run captured.

title: Step 7 tells an auditor the diff "is not this slug's" in the standing where the tool has just said only that nothing relates the two
deliverable: Step 7 is worded from the standing it was computed from, so a known-foreign diff is refused and an unknown relation is named as unknown; whichever way the pass file goes, the brief and the standing say the same thing.
evidence: `rangeIsThisSlugs` is `branchSpec === slug && !lastPassMerged`, so it is false in the third standing too — `branchSpec: null`, where the brief's own line reads "Nothing relates <slug> to <branch> ... The range above is this branch's whatever <slug> promised", an explicit statement that the relation is unknown, not wrong. In that case step 7 now prints "Do not file a pass. The diff above is not <slug>'s", asserting as fact what the paragraph above it declined to assert, and no pass file is written. Reachable whenever the store and event log carry no record of the branch working a spec — a fresh worktree, or an audit run after the branch record is gone.

title: The `mutate` journal fix writes its finding's narrative into the source, which CLAUDE.md names as a third copy that cannot be executed
deliverable: The comments keep only what a reader of the file cannot derive — that restoring and forgetting must be one act, and that a stale journal is reported rather than guessed at — and the history goes where the repository already keeps it.
evidence: CLAUDE.md: "Never close an audit finding by writing its rationale into the source. The finding lives in `docs/audits/`, its fix lives in the code, and every behavioural claim it makes lives in a test." The `putBack` comment is ten lines narrating the pass-3 finding — which path used to clean up, which brief armed it, what the next run then did — and `recoveryStanding`'s carries the measurement "89 lines of a committed file, in a clean tree, with one stderr line to say so". Every behavioural claim in both is already a passing test in `scripts/mutate.test.ts`, and the narrative is already in the commit message and the audit record. Two findings of exactly this shape are already filed unreviewed on this spec (pass 1 on specDoc.ts:31, pass 2 on audit.ts:429-435 and its twin in the test file), so the pattern is growing rather than being caught.

title: The mutation manifest's path is not keyed to the pass, so a later pass inherits the previous pass's aimed entries, and the notes that would explain the sentinels are suppressed exactly then
deliverable: The manifest path carries the pass number the way the pass file does, so a new pass gets a new file and the kept-artifact rule only ever protects work done within one pass; and `manifestNotes` prints on both paths, with the kept sentence added to it rather than replacing it.
evidence: The pass file is `audit-<slug>-pass<N>.txt` and gets a fresh path each pass; the manifest is `mutations-<slug>.json` and never changes. With c10 keeping any file that exists, pass N+1's auditor is handed pass N's manifest — fully aimed, at line text judged against a different head — under a step 4 that reads "Set each entry's `file` and `find` to the line that clause is about ... then `npm run mutate`". Measured live in this pass: after aiming the manifest by hand, a second `audit-prompt audit-brief-arrives-complete` printed under "Mutation manifest —" only "This file already exists and was left alone — it is the mutation manifest from an earlier run of this brief, and yours if you have aimed it", and none of the four `manifestNotes` lines: not the "26 entry(ies)" count, not "`file` and `find` are yours, and are the whole judgement", not "A kill by any other line is the suite noticing something, not this clause proving itself". That last sentence is the whole of what four passes cost to learn, and it is dropped on the one path where the manifest in front of the auditor may not be theirs.

title: audit can record a finding but has no flag to give it evidence
deliverable: A finding recorded by tasks audit can carry evidence, so triage shows what is broken as well as what fixing it would mean. Either --evidence attaches to the open --finding the way --severity and --deliverable already do, or audit refuses a finding with no evidence the same way it refuses one with no deliverable.
evidence: parseAuditArgs routes every --evidence to the clause-scoped map regardless of position, unlike --file which is overloaded by position and attaches to the open --finding. cmdAudit then hardcodes evidence: null on every finding it creates. Hit for real: all five findings from pass 1 of task-system-small-test-fixes-to-get-feet-wet were recorded with a deliverable and no evidence, so tasks triage printed the header "evidence - what is broken:" with nothing under it and the queue could not be triaged from inside the tool. The text had to be recovered from the audit's report afterwards with tasks edit. Note the asymmetry the tool already enforces in the other direction: add and audit both refuse a finding with no --deliverable, on the grounds that a finding must say what fixing it would mean, while evidence - the half that says what is broken - cannot be supplied at all.

title: a finding's spec is discarded on write, so spec-scoped queries cannot see it
deliverable: one recorded fact answers 'which spec does this task belong to', and every spec-scoped query — list --spec, next, spec show — sees a finding filed by tasks audit
evidence: Root cause is broader than first filed. cmdAdd:591 hard-codes a finding's spec to null, so 'tasks add --kind finding --spec X' ACCEPTS the flag, reports success, and drops it — no diagnostic. cmdAudit:1880 does the same, keeping provenance only in source.spec, while cmdAudit:1853 gives an undelivered clause task a real spec. Consequences seen twice on this branch: 36 of 41 inherited records were invisible to list --spec and next, and my own measurement pass wrote 'the spec's premise is wrong by roughly 3x' into a planning document workers were told to trust. A worker re-pointing records hit it again and had to use spec add as a second step. There is also no non-interactive path from 'an agent found something' to 'it is in the branch's queue' — triage is a global interactive walk with no targeted form. This is c9's subject arriving from the side c9 originally did not name: the flag is recognised, understood, then silently discarded, which is worse than refusing it. How to apply: one recorded fact answers which spec a record belongs to; a recognised flag either takes effect or is refused. Re-pointed at f0936dc, where the old :1853/:1880 had run past the end of a file U2 shortened to 1875 lines. cmdAdd's hard-code is scripts/tasks.ts:370, cmdAudit's finding is :1622, and the undelivered clause task that does get a real spec is :1591. A third site shares the defect and was not filed: cmdImport at scripts/tasks.ts:1094 writes spec null for every imported finding too, which is how 36 of the 41 inherited records became invisible in the first place.

title: Make the audit loop cost less, measured
evidence: ROOT RECORD — the whole picture for this branch; it holds no write grant, because the last root task (tool-friction-backlog) was declined for a grant that collided with every slice beneath it. Work the members, not this. Two audits of tool-friction-backlog on 2026-08-04 were measured with npm run session-timing: pass 1 waited 15.1 of 25.2 minutes, pass 2 waited 15.5 of 39.1. The share fell from 60 percent to 40 only because pass 2 generated for twice as long — its auditor backgrounded the expensive command and then blocked on its own poll for 421 seconds, which moved when the cost was paid without reducing it. So no clause here is graded on a share. npm run mutate is 1047 of the 1836 seconds either auditor waited, 57 percent, and scripts/tasks.test.ts is 84 of the suite's 89 seconds because one test file is one vitest worker. Order: mutate-narrows-to-a-test first (c1, c2, the 57 percent), then mutate-leaves-behind-what-a-mutant-created (c3, same file, a restore gap found during tool-friction-backlog and never filed), then merge-ready-legs-run-together (c4) and task-tests-split-by-command (c5) which are independent of both. c6 is verified at audit time by running session-timing against this branch's own audit and recording absolute waiting minutes against 15.1 and 15.5. Full clause text and the per-command Targets table are in docs/specs/audit-loop-costs-less.md; tasks plan grades the set at zero defects.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 4: `merge-ready` runs its independent legs concurrently, still reports every leg in a stable order, and reaches the same verdict it reaches in series. The legs are separate processes over shared read-only state, and the command already collects every result before emitting a line, so concurrency changes nothing a caller can observe except the clock. The serial loop is `runMergeReady` at `mergeReady.ts:45`, over the `LEGS` table at `mergeReady.ts:16`; the function already collects every `LegResult` before its first `emit`, which is what makes the order a formatting choice rather than a consequence of scheduling. Measured on `da8ddb0`: 89s tests, 16.2s audit-status, 7.8s doctor, 4.5s tsc, 1.0s layer-check, serially ~120s — and the pass-2 auditor paid 123s of it in the foreground.
deliverable: `merge-ready` runs its independent legs concurrently, still reports every leg in a stable order, and reaches the same verdict it reaches in series. The legs are separate processes over shared read-only state, and the command already collects every result before emitting a line, so concurrency changes nothing a caller can observe except the clock. The serial loop is `runMergeReady` at `mergeReady.ts:45`, over the `LEGS` table at `mergeReady.ts:16`; the function already collects every `LegResult` before its first `emit`, which is what makes the order a formatting choice rather than a consequence of scheduling. Measured on `da8ddb0`: 89s tests, 16.2s audit-status, 7.8s doctor, 4.5s tsc, 1.0s layer-check, serially ~120s — and the pass-2 auditor paid 123s of it in the foreground.
evidence: The code and its targets hold at unit level: KILLED a mutant that serialized the legs (awaited each before starting the next — the held-open resolvers never all appear and the declaration-order target times out) via "every leg is reported, in declaration order, whatever order they finish in", and KILLED status === 0 || status === 1 via "one red leg among green ones still fails the gate and names only itself", each 1 failed of 26. But the clause's acceptance criterion — "reaches the same verdict it reaches in series" — fails on the machine the spec's own numbers were measured on: two consecutive npm run tasks -- merge-ready runs on a clean tree (42s and 43s wall, against ~120s serial) both went red on the npm test leg with 5000ms test timeouts (scripts/modportal.test.ts "opts an approved mod in and back out" both times, scripts/tasks/doctor.test.ts "default-store writes stay silent" once), while standalone npm test passed 1583/1583 twice the same hour. The legs are separate processes over shared read-only state, but the CPU is shared state too: npm test already saturates 24 threads, and tsc + audit-status + doctor on top push spawn-heavy 5s-budget tests over their timeout. The serial gate ran npm test uncontended and would have passed. Filed as a finding with the fix's meaning.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 5: No single test file accounts for more than a quarter of `npm test`, and `npm test` completes in at most half the 89 seconds measured on `da8ddb0`. Verified by measurement, not by an assertion: a wall-clock threshold pinned in a test is a flake on someone else's machine, and CLAUDE.md's own five-minute rule is a measured property for the same reason. The auditor re-runs it and records the number.
deliverable: No single test file accounts for more than a quarter of `npm test`, and `npm test` completes in at most half the 89 seconds measured on `da8ddb0`. Verified by measurement, not by an assertion: a wall-clock threshold pinned in a test is a flake on someone else's machine, and CLAUDE.md's own five-minute rule is a measured property for the same reason. The auditor re-runs it and records the number.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-05, 24-thread machine. Second half holds: npm test = 33.08s vitest duration (35s wall), well under the 44.5s ceiling — a 63% cut from 89s. First half fails: by the spec's own measure (file seconds against suite seconds, the "84 of the suite's 89"), scripts/tasks/audit.test.ts ran 32.7s inside the full run (json reporter, endTime-startTime) and 22.99s solo (npx vitest run scripts/tasks/audit.test.ts: Duration 22.99s), with handoff.test.ts at 32.1s and records.test.ts at 31.7s beside it — 70-99% of npm test, not under a quarter. One file is one vitest worker, so a ~23s file is a floor the suite cannot drop below; the split moved test names, not runtime, and the runtime concentrates where the tests spawn a subprocess per CLI call. The branch measured the same fact itself and filed remediation as task-suite-spawn-costs (open): its stdin-seam part is what would discharge this half.
reason: Consciously abandoned under the strict reading: handoff.test.ts is 16.2s of a 25.2s wall, and shrinking it further means faking the git subprocesses that are the thing it tests. npm test itself is at 25.8s against the 44.5s ceiling. We will reevaluate handoff and its tests if npm test becomes an issue in the future.

title: cmdMergeReady decodes each captured stdout/stderr chunk independently, so a multibyte character split across pipe-chunk boundaries becomes U+FFFD in the replayed leg output
deliverable: Leg output is byte-accurate however the OS chunks it: accumulate Buffer chunks and decode once on close, or setEncoding('utf8') on both streams so Node carries partial UTF-8 sequences across chunk boundaries. One line either way, in the run closure of cmdMergeReady.
evidence: In the run closure of cmdMergeReady (scripts/tasks/mergeReady.ts, spawn branch): child.stdout.on('data', (chunk: Buffer) => { output += chunk }) — the += calls toString('utf8') per chunk, and pipe reads split at 64KiB with no respect for character boundaries, so a leg whose output crosses a boundary mid-character replays with replacement characters. Cosmetic while leg output stays ASCII; wrong the first time a test name or path carries non-ASCII, which test names in this repo already may. Fixed when a split multibyte sequence round-trips whole.

title: the concurrent merge gate reproducibly fails its npm test leg on a clean tree, so it reaches a different verdict than the serial gate it replaced
deliverable: merge-ready goes green on a tree whose npm test passes standalone, and stays concurrent where that is compatible: either the npm test leg keeps enough of the machine (start the four cheap legs after it finishes or cap vitest workers under the gate), or the timeout-bound spawn tests stop being timeout-bound under load (raise their budgets or, better, land the stdin seam already filed as task-suite-spawn-costs so audit/triage/doctor/modportal-style tests stop paying a subprocess per call). Fixed when two consecutive merge-ready runs on a clean passing tree report every leg green.
evidence: Two consecutive npm run tasks -- merge-ready runs on the same clean tree (commit 8dd7ddc), 2026-08-05 on the 24-thread machine the spec's own measurements come from: run 1 red with 2 timeouts (scripts/modportal.test.ts "opts an approved mod in and back out, recording the choice as intent" and scripts/tasks/doctor.test.ts "default-store writes stay silent about their own dirtiness, and warn once over stale uncommitted state", both "Test timed out in 5000ms"), run 2 red with the modportal timeout again — 2 for 2. Standalone npm test the same hour: 1583/1583 passed, twice (33.08s and a json-reporter run). The failing tests spawn subprocesses with 5s budgets; npm test's workers saturate the cores and the concurrent tsc/audit-status/doctor legs add the load that tips them. The serial gate gave npm test the machine to itself, so this red is introduced by the concurrency change, not by any test this branch wrote — clause 4's "reaches the same verdict it reaches in series" is the property this breaks.

title: the merge gate's npm-test leg races a 4x longer per-test clock than the identical CI leg, so a test regressing into the 5-20s band passes merge-ready and fails CI
deliverable: The gate exists to predict CI's verdict, and mergeReady.ts:26 gives its npm-test leg --testTimeout=20000 while .github/workflows/test.yml:35 runs plain npm test at vitest's 5000ms default on both OSes (no testTimeout in vite.config.ts). Fixing it means re-aligning the clocks once the divergence matters: either the gate names any test that only passed with headroom so a false green is visible, or the headroom is removed when the leg stops sharing the box (e.g. the leg runs last alone, or contention shrinks further). Until then a 5-20s test regression is invisible to merge-ready and red in CI.
evidence: Both gate runs this pass were green with the CI-equivalent standalone runs also green, so the window is currently empty; the divergence is structural, in the lenient direction only, and was introduced by afa3853 as the deliberate fix for pass 1's HIGH contention finding — measured twice red before, twice green after.
reason: The divergence is the documented fix for pass-1's HIGH: the gate's five contending legs need headroom an idle CI runner does not. It fails only in the lenient direction — CI still catches a test regressing into the 5-20s band — and that band is currently empty.

title: Record a full audit pass from a file instead of through argv
deliverable: Clause 13. tasks audit <spec> reads the same --proof/--evidence/--finding flags from a file, so a pass carrying evidence specific enough to re-run is not rationed by the Windows 8191-character command line. The store write is already one operation; only the transport changes. The findings half needs nothing - filing findings without --proof already appends no pass, which clause 16 pins. Disjoint from every other slice; nothing blocks it.
evidence: Two sessions hit the limit. The tasks-roadmap pass composed roughly 13k characters of argv over nine clauses plus five findings and the shell answered 'The command line is too long.' - nothing ran, and the failure arrives only after the whole invocation is composed. The droptables pass then compressed its evidence to fit, which is the wrong pressure: the command asks for evidence a next pass can re-run and then rations how much of it there is room for. Splitting the pass is not an escape, because a clause left ungraded in a pass records unknown.

title: Audit-prompt drift check and the isolation question
deliverable: A discussion with a recorded outcome, split out of task-suite-spawn-costs on 2026-08-05. Two questions: (1) should the audit-prompt brief surface npm test's wall time and largest-file share so an auditor sees test drift — spawn-heavy tests accumulating until one file dominates the suite again — without hunting for it, and if so what shape does that check take; (2) is turning vitest isolation off worth its risks here — transform+import sums are per-file isolation duplication, but tests patch console, process.exitCode and cwd, and at least one test depends on a fresh module registry per file (the warn-once flag). Neither question is code until the discussion lands as a decision.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-05: vitest reports tests 205s summed against a 31s wall; transform 15s and import 25s are isolation re-imports that never touch the wall. The drift case is real: scripts/tasks.test.ts grew to 84s of an 89s suite before audit-loop-costs-less split it.

title: Auto-save, export and load
evidence: There is no player save at all today. serializeSave is called in exactly two places and both write # save test fixtures; there is no /save, no storage, and no task in the store that builds one, which is why offline-progression currently defers its own trigger to a branch that does not exist. This task is that branch. It builds: a save store seam (localStorage in the browser, a file under the CLI, so the thing is exercisable before src/ui exists), autosave on a cadence, a setting for that cadence where 0 means never, and /export and /import which print the current save and take one back. The import route half exists already -- /dsl save <id> <body> stages a section and /load <id> loads one -- so export/import may alias those rather than growing a second spelling. Two gaps it must close or declare: no settings store exists anywhere in src/ or scripts/, so the autosave cadence has nowhere to live yet; and localStorage needs a browser, so the seam is what lands now with the browser implementation arriving with gui-rebuild. Hard constraint from offline-progression: loading or importing a save must never advance time. A save has to load back to exactly what was written, or an import of a week-old export would burn the offline cap before the player saw it. Filed 2026-08-05.

title: Balance pass driven by agent playtesters

title: a requires edge to a declined or missing task blocks its dependent forever, and no test covers either
deliverable: Decide whether a declined requirement blocks, then make isBlocked say so and pin it with a test. isBlocked is task.requires.some((id) => byId.get(id)?.state !== 'done'), so only done unblocks: declining a task strands every dependent permanently, and the optional chain makes an id that is not in the store block by the same route. fixNowQueue filters on !isBlocked, so next returns nothing and names nothing - the read goes silent rather than reporting what it could not determine, which is c1's subject. The BLOCKED computation is in the spec's Carried forward list, so this is untested behaviour in code being kept, not in code being deleted.
evidence: Found while re-pointing the 38 spec members on 2026-08-02, as a live constraint rather than a hypothetical: U8 and U9 had thirteen dependents between them and both had to be emptied before either could be declined, because declining first would have stranded all thirteen with no diagnostic anywhere in the tool. The three isBlocked cases at scripts/lib/taskStore.test.ts:196-211 use only open and done requirements, so declined, in-progress, unreviewed and missing have never been exercised. The in-progress half of this gap is pass2-a-h1's surviving mutation; the declined and missing halves are unfiled until now.

```html
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml" />
```

All three are root-absolute. itch.io's own HTML5 docs (https://itch.io/docs/creators/html5) and
its community support threads state that an HTML5 upload is served from a subdirectory of
itch's CDN, and an absolute path (`/...`) causes the browser to request outside that
subdirectory and 404 — the fix is `base: './'` so every path stays relative to
`index.html`'s own location. This is a known, specifically-Vite gotcha (confirmed by multiple
independent reports of the same symptom with Vite defaults). I did not push a build to itch to
reproduce the 404 directly — that would violate this audit's "never publish" constraint — but
the mechanism is externally documented, not inferred, and the absolute paths are directly
verified in the built artifact this pipeline emits.

This does not appear to regress Capacitor's Android build: Capacitor's WebView serves `dist/`
from a virtual host root (`https://localhost/`), so root-absolute paths already resolve
correctly there. Switching to `base: './'` should fix itch.io without affecting Android, since
relative paths resolve correctly from any serving root.

**Fix**: add `base: './'` to `vite.config.mjs`, rebuild, and diff `dist/index.html` to confirm
the paths become relative before the next tag push.
reason: Fixed: base:'./' set; verified relative paths in build-deployment-2026-07-30.md Verified-closed (BD-H1).

title: the pipeline has no gate against publishing a non-functional placeholder, and today's build is exactly that
evidence:
**Verified.** `src/main.tsx:6-20` renders a single fixed-size div with the text
`"Universalis — text-adventure GUI pending"` and nothing else — no import of the runtime, no
session, no router. This is a known, intentional placeholder (`src/ui` does not exist yet per
`docs/audits/systems.json`'s own note on the User Interface system), not a bug in this system's
files — but the *consequence* is squarely this system's: `.github/workflows/publish.yml` builds
and ships whatever `src/main.tsx` produces, unconditionally, to both itch.io and a GitHub
Release APK, on any `v*` tag push. There is no smoke test, no manual approval step, and no
check anywhere in the pipeline that the emitted artifact is more than a static placeholder div.

I built `dist/` locally and confirmed this is precisely what a tag push would ship right now:
opening `dist/index.html`'s app would render only the placeholder text, full-screen, with no
game content reachable — `public/content/` only holds `gui/locales/en.json` and
`universes/index.json` (`["base"]`, an empty manifest with no matching universe files
anywhere), and nothing in `main.tsx` fetches or renders it.

This is a cross-system finding: the defect's owner is System 4 (User interface, "pending the
GUI rebuild"), but the risk — a release pipeline that will happily publish a placeholder as a
real release, with no gate to catch it — belongs to Build & deployment. Recorded here rather
than left implicit, per the instruction to establish what the deployed artifact currently *is*.

**Fix direction**: not "fix the UI" (out of this system's scope) but give the pipeline a
minimal acceptance check — e.g., a post-build smoke assertion (headless load, assert the root
element contains more than the known placeholder string) that fails the workflow rather than
publishing silently. Cheap insurance against exactly this scenario recurring once the real UI
lands and a future regression reintroduces a blank/broken render.

title: Android's version is hardcoded and has no relationship to `package.json`'s version
evidence:
**Verified.** `android/app/build.gradle:10-11`:

```gradle
versionCode 1
versionName "1.0"
```

`variables.gradle` and `build.gradle` contain no reference to `package.json`'s `"version":
"0.1.0"` (package.json:4), and no CI step reads or writes either value against the other.
`versionCode` has been `1` since project inception (`android/` was last touched, in full, by
`8465481`/`bda44e5` — see M1's table — long before the current version-0.1.0 state), which
means an Android package manager or side-loader has no way to tell two successive published
APKs apart: both would report `versionCode 1`. This is the manually-kept-in-sync pattern
CLAUDE.md's mission statement calls out directly, except worse — currently *nobody* keeps it in
sync, by hand or otherwise.

**Fix**: derive `versionCode`/`versionName` from `package.json` at build time (a small Gradle
snippet reading the JSON, or a CI step that `sed`s the two fields before `assembleRelease`),
so there is one version number, not two silently-independent ones.
reason: Fixed: versionCode/versionName now derived from package.json, confirmed in build-deployment-2026-07-30.md Verified-closed.

title: `playwright-core` is an unused devDependency
evidence:
**Verified.** `grep -r "playwright"` across the whole tracked tree (excluding
`node_modules`/lockfile) matches only `package.json` and `package-lock.json` — no source file,
script, or test imports it. Cross-checked `package-lock.json`: `playwright-core` has no
`dependencies` entry pointing to it from any other installed package (i.e. it's not a transitive
requirement of something else, such as `vitest`'s browser mode) — it is a direct, standalone
devDependency doing nothing. `git log -S"playwright-core" package.json` traces it to `35121b2`
("Implement balanced enemy combat editor"), a commit whose subject has no obvious connection to
browser automation, consistent with an accidental or exploratory addition that was never wired
up or cleaned up.

**Fix**: remove it, or if it's earmarked for the eventual reintroduction of the `window.__test`
browser harness (per CLAUDE.md's UI section), say so — an unused ~large native-binary
devDependency with no comment or backlog entry explaining its presence reads as dead weight.
reason: Unused devDependency, trivial cleanup nobody will prioritize soon.

title: `tsconfig.node.tsbuildinfo` is committed to git
evidence:
**Verified.** `git ls-files tsconfig.node.tsbuildinfo` returns the file — it is tracked.
`.gitignore` has no `*.tsbuildinfo` entry. It is also stale: its mtime and last commit
(`ee51578`) predate this audit's build run, and running `npm run build` (`tsc && vite build`)
did not regenerate it — the root `tsc --noEmit` invocation used by the build script does not
build the referenced `tsconfig.node.json` project in `-b` mode, so this file is dead weight

**Fix**: add `*.tsbuildinfo` to `.gitignore` and `git rm` the tracked copy.
reason: Fixed: no tracked tsbuildinfo remains, confirmed in build-deployment-2026-07-30.md Verified-closed.

title: `vite.config.mjs` itself is outside the type-check gate
evidence:
**Verified.** Root `tsconfig.json`'s `include` is `["src", "scripts"]`; `tsconfig.node.json`'s
`include` is `["capacitor.config.ts"]` only. `vite.config.mjs` — one of this system's own
declared paths, and the file responsible for H1 above — is covered by neither project, so
`tsc --noEmit` never looks at it (and `allowJs` is `false` at the root regardless). Low
practical impact today (the file is 27 lines and has no import errors), but notable given that
`50a4f41`, one of the seven commits under audit, closed exactly this kind of gap for `scripts/`
on the stated reasoning that an untype-checked build-relevant file "shipped silently" broken.
`capacitor.config.ts` gets this coverage via `tsconfig.node.json`; `vite.config.mjs` does not,
for no principled reason found in the config — it's simply a `.mjs` file and neither `include`
array reaches root-level `.mjs`/`.js` config files.

**Fix**: add `vite.config.mjs` (and, if desired, `postcss.config.js`/`tailwind.config.js`) to
`tsconfig.node.json`'s `include`, or accept the gap explicitly as low-value given the file's
size and change frequency.
reason: Fixed: vite.config now inside a type-checked project, confirmed in build-deployment-2026-07-30.md Verified-closed.

title: the Android CI job re-implements the `sync` npm script instead of reusing it
evidence:
**Verified.** `package.json:11` already defines `"sync": "npm run build && cap sync"`. The
`android` job in `publish.yml:37-39` performs the same two steps inline instead:

```yaml
- run: npm run build
- run: npx cap sync android
```

Functionally near-identical (the npm script syncs all platforms; the workflow scopes to
`android` specifically, which `cap sync android` supports as an argument to the existing
script's `cap sync` call). Minor duplication of the same "build then sync" sequence in two
places — if the `sync` script ever grows a step (a pre-sync content check, say), the workflow
silently keeps skipping it, which is the exact kind of hand-synced drift the audit prompt asks
to flag as a place a simpler existing pattern should have been reused.

**Fix**: `npm run sync -- android` in the workflow, or accept the duplication as intentional
(CI wants only the Android platform, the local script wants both) and drop this as noise.
reason: Fixed: android job now calls npm run sync, confirmed in build-deployment-2026-07-30.md Verified-closed.

title: (informational, not actionable) — `npm audit` findings are all dev-tooling-only
evidence:
**Verified.** `npm audit --json` reports 6 vulnerabilities (3 high, 3 critical): `tar` (via
`@capacitor/cli`), `brace-expansion` (transitive), `concurrently`→`shell-quote` (critical), and
`postcss` (via the Tailwind build toolchain). All four root packages are `devDependencies` or
build-time-only tools; none ship inside `dist/` (verified: `dist/assets/*.js` is Vite's
production bundle, and none of `tar`/`shell-quote`/`concurrently`'s code paths are reachable
from the app running in a browser — they only execute on a developer's or CI runner's machine).
Reporting honestly per the audit prompt's instruction not to inflate transitive dev-only
findings: **no user-facing or production security exposure found.** Worth a routine
`npm audit fix`/dependency bump pass at some point (the `@capacitor/cli` fix is a semver-major

`^6.2.1`), but this is maintenance, not a defect introduced by the audited commits.
reason: Informational only per its own title; no production exposure found.

title: this system's path membership is dominated by commits that never touch its actual pipeline
evidence:
**Verified.** `git show --stat` against each of the 7 audited commits, filtered to this
system's declared paths, shows all 7 touched **only** `package.json` or `tsconfig.json` — never
`.github/workflows/publish.yml`, `android/`, `capacitor.config.ts`, or `vite.config.mjs`:

| Commit | File(s) touched in this system |
| --- | --- |
| `50a4f41` | `tsconfig.json` (add `scripts` to `include`) |
| `3d1c389` | `package.json` (remove 2 script entries) |
| `5e6eceb` | `package.json` (remove 1 script entry) |
| `542f994` | `package.json` (remove 1 script entry) |
| `ee8c06e` | `package.json` (add 2 script entries) |
| `2905b41` | `package.json` (add 1 script entry) |
| `2e05502` | `package.json` (add 1 script entry) |

Every one of these is really **Testing procedure** work (the readability-gate build-and-retire
arc, documented in `docs/readability-gate/deliverable-log.md`) or **DSL/repo-wide tooling**
work, expressed as an edit to a shared config file. Confirmed the actual pipeline is untouched
further back than the audit window: `git log -1 -- .github/workflows/publish.yml android
capacitor.config.ts vite.config.mjs` resolves to `bda44e5`, and `git merge-base --is-ancestor
bda44e5 83d81d2` succeeds — meaning none of the four files that define the actual web/Android
pipeline have changed even once since *before* the previous recorded baseline. This system's
audit trigger fired entirely on noise from a neighboring system.

This is the flip side of CLAUDE.md's "keep independent systems independent": `package.json` and
`tsconfig.json` are legitimately shared infrastructure (every system's scripts and type
coverage live there), but attributing 100% of their edits to *this* system means Build &
deployment's audit budget is spent by whichever system happens to edit a script entry fastest,
while the pipeline that actually deploys the game can go unaudited indefinitely as long as
nobody touches it — which is exactly what's been happening.

**Fix direction**: narrow this system's ownership of `package.json`/`tsconfig.json` to the keys
that are actually build/deploy-relevant (e.g. the `build`/`sync`/`preview` scripts and the
`include`/`references` compiler fields), or accept `package.json`/`tsconfig.json` as
genuinely cross-cutting and stop assigning them to a single system in `systems.json`. Either
way, this is a `systems.json` design call for the user, not a code fix — flagged here as
evidence, not resolved.
reason: Resolved: ownership corrected, confirmed "Correctly removed" in build-deployment-2026-07-30.md Verified-closed.

title: third-party publish actions are pinned to floating tags, not commit SHAs, and three of them handle secrets
evidence:
**Reasoned**, from reading `.github/workflows/publish.yml` line by line. Three third-party
(non-`actions/`, non-`github/`) actions are referenced by mutable version tags:

- `josephbmanley/butler-publish-itchio-action@v1.0.3` (publish.yml:19) — receives
  `BUTLER_CREDENTIALS`.
- `r0adkll/sign-android-release@v1` (publish.yml:44) — receives the base64 signing key, alias,
  keystore password, and key password (publish.yml:46-49), i.e. everything needed to sign a
  release APK as this app.
- `softprops/action-gh-release@v1` (publish.yml:52) — has implicit `GITHUB_TOKEN` access to
  create/attach release assets.

A tag ref (`v1`, `v1.0.3`) can be moved by the upstream maintainer (or by an attacker who
compromises their account) to point at different code without the pin in this repo changing.
Since two of these three actions receive live secrets that can publish to itch.io or sign an
APK as this app, this is a real supply-chain surface, not a style nit. `actions/checkout@v4`,
`actions/setup-node@v4`, `actions/setup-java@v4` are lower-risk (GitHub-maintained, no secrets
passed) but share the same floating-tag pattern.

**Fix**: pin the three third-party actions to a full commit SHA (`uses:
owner/repo@<40-char-sha> # vX.Y.Z` for readability), per GitHub's own supply-chain hardening
guidance. GitHub-maintained actions are lower priority but the same treatment is cheap.
reason: Fixed: third-party actions pinned to commit SHAs, confirmed in build-deployment-2026-07-30.md Verified-closed (BD-M2+M3).

title: no explicit `permissions:` block in `publish.yml`
evidence:
**Reasoned.** Neither the workflow nor either job declares a `permissions:` block
(publish.yml:1-55), so both jobs run with whatever the repository/organization's default
`GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions are — a setting outside this repo, and therefore not verifiable from
here. `softprops/action-gh-release@v1` needs `contents: write` to attach the APK to a release;
the `web` job needs no GitHub API access at all (it only talks to itch.io via `BUTLER_CREDENTIALS`).
Relying on an implicit, externally-configured default is exactly the kind of ambient-scope
setup GitHub's own security hardening guide recommends against — a future org-level default
flip, or a new step accidentally added to either job, inherits whatever the default grants
with no visible ceiling in this file.

**Fix**: add an explicit `permissions:` block scoped per job — e.g. `contents: read` at the
workflow level, overridden to `contents: write` only on the `android` job's release-attach step
(or the whole `android` job).
reason: Fixed: permissions: block added, confirmed in build-deployment-2026-07-30.md Verified-closed (BD-M2+M3).

title: the signed release APK is built in development configuration and points its WebView at a dev server
evidence:
`capacitor.config.ts:3`, `package.json` (`"sync": "npm run build && cap sync"`),
`.github/workflows/publish.yml:44`.

```ts
const isDev = process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production';
const config: CapacitorConfig = {
  …,
  ...(isDev && { server: { url: 'http://10.0.2.2:5173', cleartext: true } }),
};
```

`npm run build` sets `NODE_ENV=production` **inside the Vite process only**. `cap sync` is a separate
process in the same `&&` chain, and the android job sets no environment, so it reads
`NODE_ENV === undefined` and takes the dev branch. Reproduced with the exact environment the workflow
provides:

```
--- config as CI's `cap sync` sees it (NODE_ENV unset) ---
NODE_ENV=undefined
{ "appId": "org.universalis.rpg", "appName": "UniversalisRPG", "webDir": "dist",
  "server": { "url": "http://10.0.2.2:5173", "cleartext": true } }

--- with NODE_ENV=production ---
{ "appId": "org.universalis.rpg", "appName": "UniversalisRPG", "webDir": "dist" }
```

The local synced artefact confirms the same output reaches the build:
`android/app/src/main/assets/capacitor.config.json` carries `"url": "http://10.0.2.2:5173"`.

`cap sync` bakes that into the APK's assets. `10.0.2.2` is the Android emulator's alias for the host's
loopback; on any real device it resolves to nothing routable. The published APK — assembled, signed
with the release key, and attached to the GitHub Release by `publish.yml:52-62` — therefore ignores its
own bundled `dist` and tries to load a dev server that does not exist. It also ships with cleartext
HTTP enabled, and Capacitor emits a network-security config permitting it.

Nothing catches this: the workflow's success does not depend on the app loading, and the tracked tree
holds no synced config to review (`android/app/.gitignore` excludes the build output, correctly).

**Fix.** Make the release path explicit rather than ambient — set `NODE_ENV: production` on the
android job (or gate on a dedicated flag), and assert the absence of `server` in the synced
`capacitor.config.json` before `assembleRelease`. An ambient default that produces a *broken* release
when unset is the wrong direction for the default to fail in; `isDev` should have to be asked for.

This is the same shape as **BD-H2**, still open from 2026-07-28: a tag push publishes something that
cannot work. That one ships the placeholder GUI; this one ships an APK that would not render even a
finished GUI. Both want the same gate.

title: `.gitattributes` justifies itself with a claim `4b6e383` made false in the same commit
evidence:
`.gitattributes:1-3` says the index keeps LF "so a checkout on any platform parses the same bytes",
and `test.yml:15` justifies the Windows matrix leg as the place a CRLF checkout is seen. Both cannot be
load-bearing at once: with `* text=auto eol=lf` in effect, both runners check out identical bytes, so
the Windows leg never sees CRLF. The real CRLF guard is the in-memory synthesis in
`integration.test.ts:15`, which `4b6e383` added and which is correct. This is TP-L2 of
`docs/audits/testing-procedure-2026-07-30.md` seen from the other side; recorded here because
`.gitattributes` is this system's file and carries half the false pair. The Windows leg is still worth
keeping — it covers `posix()`, tsx and vitest on the development platform — the comment just names the
wrong reason.
reason: Cosmetic comment/rationale mismatch in .gitattributes, no functional impact.
