title: merge-ready reports "every leg passed" on a planning branch whose own spec was never audited
deliverable: A planning branch is exactly the shape the spec describes: it ships a deliverable under its own spec and then writes a spec for a later branch. `merge-ready` grades one spec, whichever `resolveActiveSpec` picked, and on a worktree branch (`claude/<topic>-<hash>`, this repo's convention) the branch-name route misses and the event-log route picks the most recently written spec — the plan, because planning happens last. `specAuthoredHere` then turns that spec's two red legs green and drops the clauses leg entirely, so the gate says "merge-ready: every leg passed / then merge <branch> into main" while the spec the branch actually delivered is never mentioned and its clauses are never graded. Before this branch the same misresolution produced a red gate, which is loud and wrong; it is now green and wrong, and the false green is on the one gate that certifies a branch. Fixing it means merge-ready either grading every spec this branch touched, or naming the spec it resolved and how (`resolveActiveSpec` already returns that note and merge-ready discards it) so a reader can see it graded the wrong one.
evidence:
Reproduced end to end with a fixture in a temp dir. Store built with `npm run tasks -- add ... --store <tmp>/tasks.jsonl --specs-dir <tmp>/specs --branch claude/topic-abc`: spec real-work with member real-slice taken to done (a real deliverable), then spec plan-for-later with members plan-a and plan-b left open (the plan). Both spec files written into <tmp>/specs; neither has an audit pass.
`npm run tasks -- next --store <tmp>/tasks.jsonl --specs-dir <tmp>/specs --branch claude/topic-abc` prints `spec inferred from the event log: plan-for-later - the most recent spec written from claude/topic-abc`, so the plan shadows the delivered spec (context.ts:236, lastSpecWrittenFromBranch).
`npm run tasks -- merge-ready --store <tmp>/tasks.jsonl --specs-dir <tmp>/specs --branch claude/topic-abc` then prints `spec  ok  pass - this branch wrote plan-for-later as a plan for a later branch and worked none of its 2 member(s), so it owes neither them nor a clause`, no clauses leg, `merge-ready: every leg passed`, `then merge claude/topic-abc into main`. real-work is never named and its clause is never graded.
On the base commit the same fixture is red on both legs by inspection of the diff: without the mergeReady.ts:103 early return, `openMembers` is [plan-a, plan-b] so the spec leg fails, and `auditPasses` is 0 so the clauses leg fails.

title: the specAuthoredHere seam is untested, and an unresolvable base ref reads as "this branch wrote the spec"
deliverable: `authoredAsPlan` is pure and tested, `standingLegs` consumes an injected `specAuthoredHere` and is tested, and the line that computes one from the other — `git.fileAt(baseBranch, specFile(config, spec)) !== null` at mergeReady.ts:218 — is covered by nothing. `git.fileAt` returns null both when the file is absent from the base branch and when git cannot answer at all, so a `--base-branch` typo or a checkout without the base ref reads every all-open spec as authored here and turns both legs green. The sibling decision three lines below documents the same permissive default for `baseMoved` ("Unknown resolves to 'has not moved'"); this one is undocumented and lands on a stronger claim, in the positive voice ("this branch wrote X as a plan"). Fixing it means distinguishing "git could not answer" from "the file is not there" at the seam and failing closed on the first, plus the one real-git test CLAUDE.md's testing note asks for to prove the seam itself.
evidence: Untested: `npm run inspect -- "import('./lib/git.ts').then(g => ({ real: g.fileAt('main','docs/workflow.md') !== null, missingFile: g.fileAt('main','docs/specs/planning-branch-friction.md') !== null, missingRef: g.fileAt('no-such-branch','docs/workflow.md') !== null }))"` returns `{ real: true, missingFile: false, missingRef: false }` — the last two are indistinguishable. title: U3 flip the polarity: reads always answer, writes refuse only malformed input

title: Process defects are countable, so a planner can ask how well the system is working
deliverable: Give each process-defect class its own event op, following the decision and spec-* precedents, so tasks log --op <class> answers without text matching and the record survives the spec it was found on. Candidate classes from the run's spec: spec defect, design question, tool friction, silent guess. Pair it with the denominator query, because a count with no rate cannot answer the question that motivated it. Do not build a dashboard or a gate - ops plus a query.
evidence: Author's request 2026-08-06. The instances ARE recorded - four events exist against run-an-orchestrator-over-three-parallel-tasks already - but as op 'note' and op 'decision' carrying the class inside prose, which leaves three gaps. (1) Not countable by class: 'how many spec defects' means reading prose, and the precedent against exactly this is already in the repo - EVENT_OPS carries 'decision' as its own op with the stated rationale that a decision needs no text matching. (2) Bound to one spec: these are properties of the PLANNING SYSTEM, not of the run, so when that spec closes the only handle is --spec on a spec nobody will think to query. (3) No denominator, which is the one that decides the design: 'how well is the system working' is a RATE, not a count, and 5 defects means nothing without 5-across-how-many-dispatches. The denominator is already derivable from the log - specs written, clauses authored, work-prompts issued - so only the numerator is missing. Precedent for shape: spec-add/spec-remove/spec-defer/spec-done is already a family of four fine-grained ops rather than one op with a subtype field, so one op per class matches the house style. Classes are NOT yet settled - run-an-orchestrator-over-three-parallel-tasks's own open questions say a fifth may appear during the run - so this is specced after that run, using its recorded instances as the evidence for what the vocabulary should be.
reason: Superseded by the-workflow-records-what-cost-it-in-one-place-with-o, which is the same system rather than two. These were the write half (a worker calls its spec defective, at two levels) and the read half (a planner counts defects by class), filed hours apart, and the author's observation is that tool friction is the same shape as both -- an event that cost a round, logged so a future session can plan against it. Keeping them separate would have produced two channels a worker chooses between at the moment it is least able to classify, and two queries a planner has to remember to run. Every finding in their evidence survives in the successor: the dead kind 'question', blocking for free via isBlocked and requires, the decision and spec-* op precedents, and the denominator point. What the merge adds is the second axis -- fault -- and the rule that an unknowable question must not count as a defect.

title: wrapUnder computes its wrap budget from the first-line prefix and ignores the hanging indent it applies to every other line
deliverable: wrapUnder budgets from Math.max(first.length, hanging.length), with a render.test.ts case wrapping under a hanging indent wider than its first prefix and asserting every line stays inside TERMINAL_WIDTH. Cheap now, and it converts a silent over-width into an invariant the type of the function already implies. This is also the signal that the wrapping helpers are worth revisiting: the first caller that wants a continuation indented deeper than its head is the moment, and until then the current shape is fine.
evidence: Measured: wrapUnder('word '.repeat(30).trim(), '  ', ' '.repeat(60)) returns lines of length [76, 134] - the second is 56 characters past TERMINAL_WIDTH=78. The budget is Math.max(TERMINAL_WIDTH - first.length, MIN_WRAP_WIDTH), so a hanging indent longer than first is added on top of a full-width line. No caller today trips it: tree, entryRow and clauseStandingLines all pass hanging.length === first.length, specLines passes hanging <= first because column() floors the state cell at STATE_COLUMN, and blockedLines errs the safe way (first longer than hanging, giving short lines). So the invariant holds by coincidence across five call sites and is neither documented nor tested.

title: Run an orchestrator over three parallel tasks
evidence: The controlled run the author asks for before an orchestrator prompt is written: you cannot brief a role whose failure modes you have not seen. Reframed 2026-08-06 - the point is ENDURANCE, not cost. Cost is settled by delegation-experiments.md. The constraint is that supervising a worker costs the author half a day, nearly all of it reading output and saying continue, while a planning session yields a dozen specs in the same day; with 17 specced tasks and ~30 findings waiting, the human is the bottleneck and every mid-branch design question is paid at the expensive rate. title: `checkSave` never looks inside the three fields that have an inside, and `loadSave` crashes on them with a `TypeError`
evidence:
**Verified, two reproductions.** `save.ts:38-52` gives every save field a `holds` predicate. For
the ten scalar- and number-shaped fields it is a real check. For the three object-shaped fields —
`activeAction`, `player`, `activeBuffs` — it is `isObject`, which is to say no check at all. Those
are exactly the three fields with internal structure to get wrong.

The rule the file states for itself (`save.ts:28-29`):

> "A `# save` body is hand-written JSON that nothing else checks, so this is where a
> `"time":"potato"` is caught."

It catches `"time":"potato"` and misses the class that actually crashes:

| `# save` body (version 5) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `{"time":"potato"}` | `RuntimeError: save field time holds "potato"…` ✅ |
| `{"activeAction":[]}` | `RuntimeError: …not what activeAction keeps` ✅ |
| `{"activeAction":{}}` | **`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'indexOf')`** |
| `{"activeAction":{"ownerRef":"entity.oven","actionLabel":"bake","repeating":false,"healthRemaining":1000}}` | **`TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object`** |
| `{"player":{}}` | accepted; `state.player.name` is `undefined` thereafter |
| `{"activeBuffs":{"k":{}}}` | accepted, then silently pruned as "its stat undefined is not loaded" |

The first crash is `parseOwnerRef` (`save.ts:115`) on an absent `ownerRef`. The second is the
interesting one: **every id in that body is real.** The owner exists, the action label exists, so
`activeActionProblem` has nothing to prune and reaches `Object.keys(active.cadences)`
(`save.ts:127`) on an absent `cadences`. Nothing downstream can recover, because the crash is
inside the validator.

That the intent was the opposite is explicit two lines earlier: `activeActionProblem` wraps
`findActionOwner` in a `try/catch` that converts a `RuntimeError` into a warning and rethrows
anything else (`save.ts:119-122`). The author was thinking about precisely this conversion and it
is defeated by the next statement. A validator that throws a raw `TypeError` on the input class it
exists to validate has not validated it — and this is the only gate between hand-written JSON and
the resolver, since `06c2e47` routed `pruneStateForRegistry` through it for browser and disk saves
too (`scripts/play-cli.ts:320`).

**Fix**: `holds` for these three needs to be a real structural predicate, not `isObject` — for
`activeAction`, at minimum a string `ownerRef`, a string `actionLabel`, and a `cadences` object
carrying `PLAYER`. That is the same shape `activeActionProblem` already assumes; it just has to be
asserted before the assumptions are used rather than after.

title: `attemptDuration`'s floor gives one authored value three different fates
evidence:
`Math.floor(timeMs / speed)` (`stats.ts:53`) can now reach 0 for any positive `time:`, which the
pre-conversion float division could not. What happens next depends on which path reads it:

| Path | `duration === 0` |
| --- | --- |
| `armAction`, repeating | `RuntimeError` at arm time (`runtime.ts:404`) |
| `applyDueBoundaries`, deterministic non-repeating | treated as instant and completed (`runtime.ts:315`) |
| `resolveStochasticSegment` | **`RuntimeError` thrown mid-resolve** (`runtime.ts:215`) |

Reproduced for the third row with `time: 1, speed: 2000`: the action arms clean, `useAction`
resolves a zero-length first unit without complaint, and the next `resolve()` that crosses any
span throws `action entity.dummy.poke resolved a non-positive attempt duration (0)`. No load-time
check is possible because `speed` is state-dependent, so the three fates are the whole story.

Unreachable in shipped content — a 60 s action needs a speed stat above 60,000 — which is why this
is LOW rather than higher. It is listed because the divergence is not a decision anyone made; it
is what the floor did to three call sites that each already handled zero their own way.
reason: Self-described unreachable in shipped content, low severity.

title: `resourceRateRemainders` is never cleared when a resource stops having a rate

title: `PlaySession.logCursor` no longer carries information, and the one place it could is a nested session

title: the `# test` regressions cannot see the largest change in the window
evidence:
**Verified by mutation.** I dropped `toMilliUnits` from `initResources` (`effects.ts:81`), so
every pool initialises at 1/1000 of its intended level, and ran the shipped content:

```
✓ test "tutorial-island.tutorial-quest-given" passes
✓ test "tutorial-island.miki-route-full" passes
✓ test "tutorial-island.save-restores-object-owned-flags" passes
× tutorial-island health resource (Pass 2 end-to-end) …
```

All three `# test` sections pass with every pool off by 1000×, including `miki-route-full`, whose
`expect: miki-route-end` compares the whole save diff. The only thing that fails is a hand-written
TypeScript assertion at `integration.test.ts:40`.

The cause is in the fixture `2c2ccee` migrated. `miki-route-end` carries
`"resources":{"tutorial-island.health":0}` — zero is the single value invariant under a scale
change, so rescaling it was a no-op and the fixture pins nothing about the new scale. `time` was
rescaled `107.2` → `107200` and *does* discriminate, which is why a seconds/milliseconds mixup
would be caught and a units/milli-units one would not.

CLAUDE.md designates `# test` sections as *the* regression format. For the largest change in this
window that format certified nothing, and the mechanism — a fixture whose only pool value is the
one value the transformation fixes — will recur on the next scale change unless a fixture pins a
pool mid-range.
reason: Symptom of already-deferred dsl-load-path-2026-07-30-pass2-h1; same root cause and fix.

title: `ability:` means two different numbers depending on which fight path reads it
evidence:
**Verified.** One module, one stat `blow` at `2.5`, two actions differing only in `health:` vs
`target: health`. Four attempts each, starting from 100:

```
healthless (deterministic) path:  100000 -> 90000   = 2.5 per attempt
target:    (stochastic)   path:  100000 -> 92000   = 2.0 per attempt
```

A 20% difference from the same authored number. The deterministic path takes
`toMilliUnits(statValue(action.ability))` (`runtime.ts:72`) and is exact; the stochastic path goes
through `hitDamage`, which is `Math.max(minDamage, Math.trunc(attack - dr))` (`stats.ts:47`) and
quantises to whole units before `damagePool` converts up.

The `Math.trunc` predates this window, so the asymmetry is not new — but the integer conversion
made the healthless path exact while leaving the target path quantised, which widens the gap
rather than closing it, and it is the sort of thing a conversion touching every damage site was
the natural moment to reconcile. This is a measurement for the `action.health`/`target:`

title: `rng` is the one number in `GameState` the conversion left un-integered, and a fractional cursor collapses the stream
evidence:
**Verified.** `SAVE_FIELDS` validates `time` and both pool records with `isInteger` and `rng` with
`isNumber` (`save.ts:48-49`). Since the pass-2 H1 fix, `nextRandom` is
`(Math.imul(cursor.rng, MULTIPLIER) + INCREMENT) >>> 0` (`rng.ts:14`), and `Math.imul` applies
`ToInt32` to its arguments. So a save carrying `"rng":0.5` is accepted, and:

```
draws from rng=0.5    : 0.0000028742942959, 0.8275770242, 0.6524071617, 0.8374803169
draws from rng=12345  :                     0.8275770242, 0.6524071617, 0.8374803169
```

Every fractional cursor truncates to the same integer and lands on the same fixed stream one draw
later. Two saves that differ only in their `rng` fraction produce bit-identical futures. The
window's own work makes this worth fixing rather than tolerating: `5f3708d` built `SAVE_FIELDS` as
a `Record` over an exhaustive key type specifically so a field could not be forgotten, and the
table is exhaustive over *names* while remaining loose about *values* — which is the same root as
H1. `rng: isInteger` is a one-word change.

title: The five undelivered clause tasks of a superseded spec cannot be closed by any command
deliverable: POLICY QUESTION for a human: the store has no way to express that a spec was abandoned. Decide what happens to an undelivered clause task when its spec is superseded, then give the tool that verb. c5 of task-system-policy-seam answers it - drop --because closes any record - and U5 names these five as its proof, so this record is now a live acceptance test for U5 rather than an open question. Until then the five stay open and there is no non-falsifying exit.
evidence: Found while reconciling U1. Re-verified route by route on 2026-08-02, each refusing differently: decline gives 'is undelivered and cannot be declined'; done gives 'is undelivered and proof clause N is not met in the latest audit pass (pass 1)'; spec done --defer-open does not defer them at all but errors 'not done - neither done nor declined' naming all five; spec remove gives 'undelivered task(s) cannot be removed from a spec'; drop does not exist yet. Confirmed why done can never succeed: only pass 1 is recorded in the spec file and it rules clauses 1, 2, 4, 5 and 8 unmet - exactly these five - and pass 2's verdicts were never written. Two things make this worse than when it was filed. First, three of the five now describe machinery task-system-policy-seam deletes, so they can never become met on any branch: clause 1 is proof targets and check --merge, clause 4 is branch-rename protection plus the freeze baseline plus clause-id retirement, and clause 8's fifth required command is check --merge. Second, start and stop accept an undelivered task and edit does too, so the record can be claimed and annotated but not closed - the tool's only writes on it are the ones that change nothing about its being stuck. Re-run against the post-deletion tree at f0936dc on clause-1, verbatim, store confirmed unchanged after each: 'tasks decline <id> --reason ...' exits 1 with 'error: <id> is undelivered and cannot be declined' (scripts/tasks.ts:769); 'tasks spec remove task-system-real-world-friction-spec <id>' exits 1 with 'error: undelivered task(s) cannot be removed from a spec: <id>' (:989); 'tasks done <id> --commit HEAD' exits 1 with 'error: <id> is undelivered and proof clause 1 is not met in the latest audit pass (pass 1)' (:696); 'tasks drop <id> --because ...' exits 1 with 'unknown command: drop' (:1843). spec done --defer-open was not re-run: it writes across every member of the superseded spec and its refusal is already recorded, so re-measuring it risks a partial write for no new information. The deletions also split the five, which were previously treated as one shape. Three are unachievable on any branch because their subject is gone: clause 1 names proof-target execution and check --merge, clause 4 names the merge gate and the freeze baseline, clause 8's fifth required command is check --merge. The other two are not - every element clause 2 names is in the tree (done records closedCommit at :747, dirtyStoreIssue warns on an uncommitted write, workingTreeOnlyIssues reports working-tree-only state, closedCommitIssues at :302 reports an unreachable closing commit), and every element clause 5 names is printed by audit-prompt at :1173-1205. Those two are stuck only because pass 1 graded them unmet and pass 2's verdicts were never written to the superseded spec file. Recording that pass is not this sweep's to do - a verdict is an auditor's assertion, and writing one to clear a deadlock is the exact fabrication the ledger exists to prevent - but it means c5's drop is the only route for three of the five, not five of five.
reason: closed by U3, not by U5: c2's guard removal made decline --reason work on an undelivered clause task. Verified 2026-08-02 against a scratch copy of the live store on task-system-real-world-friction-spec-clause-1, which declined cleanly and reported 'declining it abandons the clause, it does not discharge it'. The deadlock was never a missing verb, so the drop --because that c5 originally specified is cut rather than built.

title: `tasks spec show --full` is dead as documented and a silent no-op when accepted, and the `## Deliverable` section it replaced left the CLI
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/commands.ts:33`, `scripts/tasks/cli.ts:25`, `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:95`

Before this branch, `tasks spec show <slug>` printed `doc.deliverableSection` unconditionally (`354682d:scripts/tasks.ts:1467`). The branch replaced that with clause standings and moved the section behind a new `--full`. `flagArities` infers a flag's arity from the token that follows it in the usage string; `spec show`'s usage ends `[--order] [--full]  (default shows clause standings; --full prints the whole ## Deliverable)`, so the token after `[--full]` is `(default` — not empty, not `--`/`[--`/`]`-prefixed — and `--full` is classified `value`. Reproduced against a scratch store:

- `tasks spec show demo-spec --full` → `error: --full needs a value`, exit 1. Same for the `tasks spec <slug> --full` shorthand.
- `tasks spec show demo-spec --full true` → works, prints the section. The literal string `true` is required and is documented nowhere.
- `tasks spec show demo-spec --full yes` → **exit 0, flag silently ignored**, standings printed. That is precisely what `cli.ts`'s own contract forbids ("a flag not named there is an error, never a silent no-op") and what `context.ts:10-12` cites as the reason `--actor` is not a global.

The same-spirit input the code handles is `tasks next --full`, which works because `[--full]` is the last token of that usage string. I ran every command's usage through `flagArities`: `spec show`'s `--full` is the only flag in the tool written `[--x]` yet inferred as taking a value.

Net effect: the whole `## Deliverable` section is no longer obtainable from the CLI by any documented route (`handoff` and `audit-prompt` print clauses only), and CI's `npm run tasks -- spec show "$SPEC_BRANCH"` on every PR now reports strictly less than before the branch. **This makes c2 unmet** — "the CLI surface is unchanged except where a clause below changes it deliberately", and no clause touches `spec show`.

**Fix:** stop `flagArities` at a prose parenthetical the way `positionalArity` already does, or move the parenthetical ahead of the flag list; add a test that runs `spec show --full` and asserts the Deliverable prose appears, so the boolean/value classification is pinned rather than inferred silently.

title: c3's "at most once per process" has no test
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/context.ts:97`, `scripts/tasks/context.ts:110`

title: c5's exact-id-wins rule has no test, and `uniqueId` manufactures the collision it guards
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/resolveIds.ts:21-25`, `scripts/tasks/context.ts:232-238`

Mutation deleting the exact-match shortcut: **SURVIVED the whole suite** (0 failed of 1312). The rule is load-bearing by construction, not by accident: `uniqueId` resolves a slug collision by appending `-2`, so the tool itself creates strict prefix pairs. **Fix:** a test with `foo` and `foo-2` in one store asserting `tasks show foo` returns `foo` and prints no resolution line.

title: `tasks list --spec <slug> --state unreviewed` hides the findings c8 exists to surface

title: `promote` silently re-homes another spec's open member, and calls an `in-progress` record closed when refusing it
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/records.ts:631-639`

Reproduced: `crossmember` open in `other-spec`; `tasks promote crossmember --spec demo-spec` → exit 0, `promoted crossmember into demo-spec`, and the record now names `demo-spec`, with no note that it left another spec. `spec add` — the verb that exists for this — reports the move it makes (`moved into spec X from Y`); `promote` does not, and its usage says it "moves unreviewed or deferred records into the spec", which is narrower than what it accepts. Separately, the refusal guard `from !== 'unreviewed' && from !== 'open'` catches `in-progress`, but the message reads "it does not reopen closed ones". `promote` also assigns `task.state` directly rather than through `transition`, so it is the one state-moving verb that never releases a claim.

**Fix:** report the previous spec on a cross-spec promote, and give the `in-progress` case its own message (or route the move through `transition`).

title: `tasks promote` prints "promoted <id>" for records it then discards
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/records.ts:629-643`

Reproduced. Scratch store with unreviewed finding `finding-one` and done task `plain`:

```
$ tasks promote finding-one plain --spec demo-spec
stdout: promoted finding-one into demo-spec
stderr: error: plain is done — promote moves unreviewed or deferred records into a spec, it does not reopen closed ones
exit 1
store after: finding-one  state=unreviewed  spec=null
```

The loop announces each promotion inside itself, but `saveStoreAndWarn` is only reached after the loop, so a refusal on any later id throws away every promotion it already reported. `done` and `decline` do not have this shape: `resolveTaskIds` settles the whole batch before either write loop begins, which is what c4's "one bad id refuses the batch before anything is written" buys. `promote` validates state inside the loop instead.

**Fix:** pre-validate every resolved record's state before mutating or printing anything, mirroring `resolveTaskIds`'s all-or-nothing contract, so the batch either promotes and reports, or refuses and reports nothing.

title: a second-pass finding filed the c7 way is stamped `pass 1`, so the pass-2 promotion guard never fires
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/audit.ts:434`, `scripts/tasks/records.ts:636`, `scripts/tasks/triage.ts:60`, `docs/workflow.md:40-44`

`cmdAudit`'s findings-only branch records `const against = doc.auditPasses.length === 0 ? 1 : doc.auditPasses[doc.auditPasses.length - 1].pass` — the *latest existing* pass, not the pass doing the filing. Reproduced end to end against a scratch spec:

```
pass 1 recorded in full            -> ### Pass 1 written
tasks audit demo-spec --finding …  -> "recorded … against pass 1"; source={"spec":"demo-spec","pass":1}; id demo-spec-pass1-…
tasks audit demo-spec --proof 1=met --finding … -> source={"spec":"demo-spec","pass":2}; id demo-spec-pass2-…

tasks promote demo-spec-pass1-a-second-pass-finding  -> promoted, silently
tasks promote demo-spec-pass2-a-verdict-carrying-…   -> "promoting a pass 2 finding, which extends what demo-spec owes"
```

`cmdPromote` and `cmdTriage` both gate that warning on `(task.source?.pass ?? 0) >= 2`, and workflow.md step 8 makes it a policy boundary: first-pass findings skip the walk and are auto-promoted; "From pass 2 on, promotion extends what the spec owes, so it waits for the human." c7 created the findings-only route precisely so a late pass does not reset verdicts — and that route is the one that loses the pass marker. This applies to this audit's own output: findings filed as the generated brief instructs would be recorded as pass 1 and fall under the auto-promote policy. (Related prior record, different case: `pass2-b-m5` already documents that `source.pass` is blind to hand-added findings; the findings-only route is new.)

**Fix:** record the pass the findings are *filed by*, not the pass they were filed against — `doc.auditPasses.length + 1` for provenance, keeping "against pass N" as the report text — or move the promotion policy off `source.pass` onto something the filing route cannot mis-stamp.

title: c5's "anywhere a command resolves a task id" is false for four inlets, and workflow.md states it as universal
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:59`, `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:212`, `scripts/tasks/architectureCmds.ts:44`, `scripts/tasks/handoff.ts:176`, `docs/workflow.md:13`

Reproduced against a store holding `long-record-identifier-one`:

| command | `long-rec` |
|---|---|
| `edit` / `start` / `stop` / `done` / `decline` / `show` / `promote` | `resolved long-rec -> long-record-identifier-one` |
| `spec add demo-spec long-rec` | `error: no such task: long-rec`, exit 1 |
| `spec remove demo-spec long-rec` | `error: no such task: long-rec`, exit 1 |
| `plan long-rec` | `no such task: long-rec`, grades nothing |
| `note "a note" --id long-rec` | **exit 0**, event written against the literal `long-rec` |

The last is the sharp one: it succeeds, so nothing signals the miss, and `tasks log --id long-record-identifier-one` will never find that note. `docs/workflow.md:13` — written by this branch — asserts "Any id may be given as a unique prefix or substring", and CLAUDE.md holds that a disagreement between the tool and that document is a defect in one of them.

**Fix:** route those four inlets through `resolveTaskIds` (report form for `plan`, refusing form for `spec add`/`spec remove`, and resolve-before-record for `note`/`decision --id` so the event names the record's real id); or narrow c5 and workflow.md to the verbs that actually resolve.

title: findings filed through `tasks import`, the second route the generated brief offers, are invisible to every c8 view
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/audit.ts:64`, `scripts/lib/taskStore.ts:345`, `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:118`, `scripts/tasks/records.ts:317`, `scripts/tasks/audit.ts:212`

`unreviewedFiledBy` reads `task.source.spec`. `cmdAudit`'s `buildFindingTask` sets `source: {spec, pass}`; `cmdImport` sets `source: null`. Filed both ways against one spec in one store:

```
demo-spec-pass1-route-a-finding   source={"spec":"demo-spec","pass":1}
demo-spec-h1                      source=null

spec show demo-spec        -> lists route A only, "awaiting triage (not members)"
list --spec demo-spec      -> lists route A only, "(filed by this spec's audit — awaiting triage)"
next                       -> "1 unreviewed finding(s) filed by demo-spec's audits await triage"
list --state unreviewed    -> both
```

The brief generated by c13 presents the routes as interchangeable: "file them in the same `tasks audit` call …, or write the report under `docs/audits/` and `tasks import <doc>`". c8 promises "An unreviewed finding filed by a spec's audit is visible from that spec"; half the sanctioned filing routes do not deliver it, and the invisible half is the one an auditor reaches for when it has a long report.

**Fix:** let `tasks import` record the provenance it files under (`--spec`/`--pass`, defaulting to the active spec, named in the brief), or stop offering `import` as an equivalent route in `audit-prompt` and workflow.md.

title: audit-prompt never checks the slug against the branch, so a merged spec's slug returns the current branch's unrelated diff
deliverable: cmdAuditPrompt resolves the diff range as merge-base(main,HEAD)..HEAD without ever relating <slug> to config.branch or to the spec's own recorded pass heads. On branch tasks-roadmap, all 11 slugs in docs/specs/ print the identical range dcc8574..6bd1699 — the slug only selects which clause list is printed beside it. task-system-refactor merged at c38657c, behind that base, so the brief for it lists roadmap.ts, roadmapCmd.ts and tasks-roadmap.md as its relevant files and asks 16 clauses to be verified against a diff containing none of their implementation. title: `tasks spec show --full` is refused, and the output `spec show` printed before this branch is now reachable only by accident
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/commands.ts:33`, `scripts/tasks/cli.ts:25`, `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:95`

At the merge-base, `tasks spec show <slug>` printed the whole `## Deliverable`. At HEAD it prints clause standings and its usage advertises `[--full]` for the old output. `--full` does not work:

```
$ npx tsx scripts/tasks.ts spec show task-system-refactor --full
error: --full needs a value
usage: tasks spec show <slug> [--order] [--full]  (default shows clause standings; --full prints the whole ## Deliverable)
```

Root cause, measured directly: `flagArities` derives arity from the usage prose, and the token after `[--full]` here is `(default`, which `cli.ts:25` does not recognise as "no value".

```
spec show arities: [["order","boolean"],["full","value"]]
next arities:      [["spec","value"],["system","value"],["severity","value"],["full","boolean"]]
```

So the same flag works on `tasks next` (last token in its usage) and is broken on `spec show`. Consequences, all reproduced: `--full true` is the only spelling that prints the deliverable; `--full yes` prints standings and silently swallows `yes` — precisely the "a flag not named there is an error, never a silent no-op" the root help promises. No test covers `spec show --full` (the only `--full` test, `scripts/tasks.test.ts:681`, is `next`). CI runs `npm run tasks -- spec show "$SPEC_BRANCH"` on every PR page, so what a reviewer sees changed — and neither the spec's clauses nor commit `4dae513`'s otherwise-exhaustive behaviour-change list mentions `spec show` at all. This contradicts c2's "the CLI surface is unchanged except where a clause below changes it deliberately"; I disagree with pass 1's `met` on c2 for this reason.

**Fix:** make `--full`'s arity unambiguous (move the parenthetical ahead of the flags, or declare arity explicitly rather than deriving it from prose), and add a test asserting `spec show <slug> --full` prints `## Deliverable` at exit 0. Since arity is inferred from a help string, one boolean-flag test per flag — or an explicit arity declaration — is what stops this recurring for the next flag someone documents with a trailing note.

title: a finding's `--evidence` is captured as clause evidence when its text begins `<digits>=`
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/audit.ts:291-296` (contract stated at `audit.ts:258-262`)

`tasks audit demo --finding X --severity low --deliverable d --evidence "404=the endpoint returns 404"` exits 1 with `error: finding "X" needs --evidence "..."`. `clauseScoped` is tried before `current` is consulted, so the finding's evidence is filed under clause 404 and the finding is then refused for having none. The module's own comment says the opposite ("once a --finding is open they attach to that finding instead and take a bare value"). Loud rather than silent, but the error names the wrong problem.

**Fix:** treat `--evidence` (like `--file` already does) as clause-scoped only while `current === null`.

title: `tasks concept "<system>"` with no concept name dies with a raw TypeError
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/architectureCmds.ts:214`

```
$ npx tsx scripts/tasks.ts concept "Task system" --paths scripts/lib/bytes.ts
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'trim')
```

`!name.trim()` is evaluated before establishing that `name` exists, and `positionalArity` admits one positional, so the body is reached. Identical at the merge-base, so not a regression — but it now sits in a module this branch created, behind a boundary (`commands.ts:115`) whose whole purpose is turning malformed input into a diagnostic. **Fix:** `!name?.trim()`.

title: `scripts/lib/bytes.ts`, written for the Task system's merge gate, is owned by Testing procedure
evidence:
**Files:** `docs/audits/systems.json` (Task system `paths`), `scripts/tasks/mergeReady.ts:3`

`tasks where scripts/lib/bytes.ts` answers `system: Testing procedure`, `imported from outside its system by: scripts/tasks/mergeReady.ts (Task system)`. c1 enumerates the eight re-homed libs by name; this branch's own new lib was not added, so it falls to Testing procedure's blanket `scripts/lib` claim and creates a fresh cross-system edge whose only consumer is the Task system. The partition is intact and `audit-status` is green either way. **Fix:** declare `scripts/lib/bytes.ts` and its test under the Task system, or record why the byte check belongs to Testing procedure.

title: `tasks promote` prints "promoted X" for records it never writes
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/records.ts:629-643`

`tasks promote beta-find gamma-done --spec demo` (gamma-done is `done`) prints to stdout `promoted beta-find into demo`, then errors on stderr and returns. Verified afterwards: `beta-find` is still `unreviewed` with `spec: null`, and no event was appended. The state check sits inside the loop, after the per-record `console.log`, while `saveStoreAndWarn` is only reached past the loop. `done`/`decline` cannot do this because `resolveTaskIds` validates the whole batch before any mutation — c4's own principle. The test at `scripts/tasks.test.ts:1716` promotes two valid ids, then refuses a single closed one, so the mixed batch is never exercised.

**Fix:** collect refusals in a first pass over the resolved records and refuse before mutating or printing, making promote all-or-nothing like done/decline; add the mixed-batch case to that test.

title: `--proof N=` naming a clause the spec does not have records an all-unknown pass, superseding verdicts, at exit 0
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/audit.ts:287-290`, `scripts/tasks/audit.ts:470-482`

Against a fixture spec whose pass 1 recorded `proof 1: met`:

```
$ tasks audit demo --proof 99=met --evidence 99=x
recorded pass 2 for demo: outstanding: c1 (unknown), c2 (unknown), c3 (unknown)
```

`### Pass 2` is written with every clause `unknown`; because `clauseStandings` reads the latest pass only, the recorded `met` no longer stands. Same for `--proof 0=met`, `--proof =met` and `--proof c1=met` (`Number('c1')` is `NaN`, so the map key matches no clause). The `met` verdict also escapes the "met requires evidence" refusal at `audit.ts:477`, because the clause is filtered out before that check runs.

This is **not a regression** — the merge-base behaves identically — but it is the exact trap c7 exists to close, reached through the one door c7 did not close, in a parser this branch otherwise hardened (it now refuses an unknown flag after `--finding`). It is not only a typo case: I drove a scratch spec through three passes and confirmed that any *partial* pass has the same effect — grading only clause 4 in pass 2 reset c1's `met — ran it` to `unknown` in the standing.

**Fix:** refuse a `--proof N=` whose N is not a numeric id present in the spec, naming the ids that exist — the treatment `--evidence` and `--file` already get for an unscoped value. Optionally carry a prior verdict forward when a pass is explicitly partial.

title: c5's fragment resolution reaches seven of the twelve places a command takes a task id
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:59`, `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:212`, `scripts/tasks/architectureCmds.ts:44`, `scripts/tasks/handoff.ts:176`, `scripts/tasks/handoff.ts:214`

`show`/`edit`/`start`/`stop`/`done`/`decline`/`promote` resolve fragments through `resolveTaskIds`. These five do not, reproduced on one fixture store:

- `tasks show beta` → `resolved beta -> beta-find`; `tasks spec add demo beta` → exit 1, `error: no such task: beta`, then lists `beta-find` as a near match.
- `tasks spec remove demo alpha-o` → same refusal.
- `tasks plan alpha-o` → exit 0, "no such task", grades nothing.
- `tasks note hello --id alpha-o` → records the event against the literal string `alpha-o`; `tasks log --id alpha-o` then answers nothing.

Commit `4dae513`'s body claims "every id position resolves a unique prefix/substring". Pass 1 graded c5 `met` on `tasks show` alone; I disagree — the clause says "anywhere a command resolves a task id".

**Fix:** route those five through `resolveTaskIds` (reporting form for the reads `plan`/`log`, refusing form for `spec add`/`spec remove`/`note --id`), or narrow c5 to the verbs it actually covers.

title: `tasks spec show --full` is rejected by the parser, and it is the only way back to the output this command had before the branch
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/commands.ts:33`, `scripts/tasks/cli.ts:25`, `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:95`

`flagArities` derives a flag's arity from the token that follows it in the usage string. In `SPEC_COMMANDS.show` the token after `[--full]` is the prose parenthetical `(default`, which is neither `--`, `[--`, `]`, nor end-of-string — so `--full` is derived as taking a **value**:

```
$ tasks spec show task-system-refactor --full
error: --full needs a value
usage: tasks spec show <slug> [--order] [--full]  (default shows clause standings; --full prints the whole ## Deliverable)
exit=1
```

Three consequences, all reproduced:
- `--full` in its documented form always exits 1. `--full true` works by accident; `--full x` is **accepted at exit 0 and silently does nothing** — precisely what the root help forbids ("a flag not named there is an error, never a silent no-op").
- `tasks spec show --full <slug>` swallows the slug as the flag's value and exits 1 printing bare usage with no error line.
- This is a **regression against base**. At `354682d` the usage was `tasks spec show <slug> [--order]` and the default output was the whole `## Deliverable` with untruncated clause text. On this branch the default is one-line standings truncated at ~100 chars with `…`, and the untruncated text is now unreachable from the CLI. `.github/workflows/test.yml:62` runs `tasks spec show` on the ubuntu leg, so the PR-page spec report changed too.

`positionalArity` (`cli.ts:44`) already stops at "the first flag or the first prose parenthetical"; `flagArities` has no such stop, so the two derivations from one usage string disagree. There is a sweep test for positional-arity drift (`scripts/tasks.test.ts:298`, whose comment names this exact failure mode — "`spec` derived 3 from prose in its own usage line and went unnoticed through two audits") but **no equivalent sweep for flag arity**, and no test anywhere references `spec show --full`.

**Fix:** teach `flagArities` the same "stop at a prose parenthetical" rule `positionalArity` already has (or move `[--full]` to the end of the usage line), and add the flag-arity twin of the existing junk-argument sweep — for every command surface, assert each boolean flag in its usage is accepted bare. Then decide deliberately whether `spec show`'s default should have changed at all; c2 promises the surface is unchanged except where a clause changes it, and no clause declares `--full`.

title: c3's "at most once per process" has no coverage; the guard survives deletion
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/context.ts:100`, `scripts/tasks.test.ts:1331`, `scripts/tasks.test.ts:152`

Mutation-tested: deleting `if (warnedStoreDirty) return;` and running `npx vitest run scripts/tasks.test.ts` gives **257 passed (257)**. The guard is untestable through the fixture that exercises it — `defaultStoreGitFixture` (`tasks.test.ts:170`) spawns a fresh `tsx` subprocess per invocation, so the module-level flag is always `false` and no test can observe a second warning in one process. The test named "…and warn once over stale uncommitted state" proves the 30-minute staleness margin only.

Pass 1 graded c3 met citing "warnedStoreDirty once per process; the warn-once-over-stale test in tasks.test.ts passes". That test does not cover the once-per-process half. This is my one direct disagreement with a pass-1 verdict: c3 is half-proved.

**Fix:** call `run(...)` twice in-process through `runInProcess` against a backdated store and assert the second call is silent, or export a reset for the flag so the property is expressible. Either way the clause's second half becomes something a mutation can break.

title: no flag value may begin with `--`, and the `--` terminator cannot rescue one
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/cli.ts:78`, `scripts/tasks/commands.ts:152`

`parseArgs` refuses any value starting with `--`, and the terminator added by c6 only makes *positionals* literal. There is no argument order that records a dashed flag value:

```
$ tasks add "t1" --evidence "--full needs a value"
error: --evidence needs a value
error: unknown flag: --full needs a value

$ tasks add "t2" --evidence -- "--full needs a value"
error: --evidence needs a value
error: unexpected argument: "--full needs a value"
```

Same for `tasks edit --title/--deliverable`, `tasks decline --reason`, and `tasks audit --finding/--evidence/--deliverable`. This bites the audit pipeline directly: filing H1 above through `tasks audit --evidence "--full needs a value"` is impossible. The workaround (never start the text with a dash) is undocumented — the only guidance, on `note`/`decision`, points at the terminator, which does not apply to values.

**Fix:** accept the next token as a value when the flag's derived arity is `value` and the token is not itself a known flag name, or honour `--` as "the next token is literal" in value position. Whichever is chosen, say so in `GLOBAL_USAGE` alongside the terminator note.

title: `tasks promote` prints promotions it did not make when the batch is refused
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/records.ts:632`

`cmdPromote` validates each record's state *inside* the write loop, after it has already printed the success line for the records ahead of it, then returns before `saveStoreAndWarn`:

```
$ tasks promote aaa bbb --spec probe
promoted aaa into probe
error: bbb is declined — promote moves unreviewed or deferred records into a spec, it does not reopen closed ones
exit=1
$ tasks show aaa
aaa  [finding/unreviewed/high]
spec: (deferred)          <- aaa was never promoted
```

Nothing is written (good), but stdout asserts a write that did not happen. `done` and `decline` get this right — `resolveTaskIds` refuses the whole batch before either touches a record — which is exactly what c4 promises and c9 says `promote` is the non-interactive form of.

**Fix:** hoist the state check into a validation pass over `resolved` before the mutation loop, so `promote` refuses with nothing printed, matching `done`/`decline`.

title: `tasks audit <spec>` with no flags on non-interactive stdin silently records an all-unknown pass over recorded verdicts
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/tasks/audit.ts:472`, `scripts/tasks/audit.ts:325`

Reproduced against a scratch store and spec:

```
$ tasks audit probe --proof 1=met --evidence 1="ran it" --proof 2=met --evidence 2="ran it too"
recorded pass 1 for probe: no clause outstanding

$ tasks audit probe < /dev/null
clause 1: first promise
met/unmet/unknown? recorded pass 2 for probe: outstanding: c1 (unknown), c2 (unknown)
exit=0

$ tasks spec show probe
clause standing (latest pass 2): outstanding: c1 (unknown), c2 (unknown)
```

`walkClausesInteractively` returns `[]` the moment `prompter.exhausted()`, the caller grades everything `unknown`, and a full pass is appended and becomes the latest — which is what the standing reads from. That is "a permanent pass that says nobody looked", the trap c7's own text names. c7 closes the *findings-without-proof* route only; the interactive route is still open, and it is the one an agent hits by typing the bare command with no TTY.

The mechanism is pre-existing (identical code at `354682d:scripts/tasks.ts:2094`), so this is not a regression — but this branch makes it materially more likely: `audit-prompt` now instructs every commissioned auditor to file through `tasks audit`, where the old CLAUDE.md prompt asked for a report.

**Fix:** refuse rather than record when the walk graded nothing and stdin was never interactive — exit 1 naming `--proof`, the same way a `met` verdict with no evidence is refused. A pass that graded zero clauses is not a pass.

title: prefix/substring id resolution is missing everywhere except the six commands that call `resolveTaskIds`, and `docs/workflow.md` promises it everywhere
evidence:
**Files:** `docs/workflow.md:13`, `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:61`, `scripts/tasks/specCmds.ts:214`, `scripts/tasks/architectureCmds.ts:45`, `scripts/tasks/handoff.ts:174`, `scripts/tasks/records.ts` (`--requires`)

`docs/workflow.md:13` states, at the head of the protocol every agent follows: "Any id may be given as a unique prefix or substring." Reproduced against the real store:

```
$ tasks show tsr-spl                                  -> resolved tsr-spl -> tsr-split          (works)
$ tasks spec add task-system-refactor tsr-spl         -> error: no such task: tsr-spl   exit=1
$ tasks plan tsr-spl                                  -> no such task: tsr-spl          exit=0
$ tasks note "probe" --id tsr-spl                     -> no record answers to tsr-spl   exit=0
```

The `--requires` case is the one with real damage, and it is used by workflow step 3:

```
$ tasks add "the dependency" --id build-the-parser
$ tasks add "the dependent" --id use-the-parser --requires build-the
added use-the-parser [task/open]
recorded 1 requirement(s) no record answers to: build-the
$ tasks show use-the-parser   -> use-the-parser [task/open] BLOCKED / requires: build-the (missing)
$ tasks doctor                -> [error] use-the-parser requires unresolved id: build-the
```

An unambiguous prefix in `--requires` creates a permanently blocked task and a standing doctor error.

**Fix:** either route `spec add`/`spec remove`/`plan`/`--id`/`--requires` through `resolveTaskIds` (the read/write emitter split it already carries covers all five), or narrow `docs/workflow.md:13` to name the commands that actually resolve. Leaving both as they are means the repository's one live protocol document is wrong about its own tool — the condition `docs/workflow.md` opens by declaring a defect.

title: a new system was declared but `tasks import` was not taught its name, so `task-system-*` audit docs import unowned
evidence:
**Files:** `scripts/lib/auditImport.ts:79`

c1 creates the `Task system`. `DOC_SYSTEM_PREFIXES` still lists only the seven older systems, and `docs/audits/systems.json` explicitly says this system's audit history lives in "the `task-system-*` … docs under `docs/audits/`". Reproduced with two identically-shaped docs:

```
$ tasks import .../task-system-2026-08-03.md
imported 1 finding(s) — no system mapping for this doc name, system left null
$ tasks import .../testing-procedure-2026-08-03.md
imported 1 finding(s)

$ tasks list --state unreviewed
task-system-2026-08-03-h1        [finding/unreviewed/high]  (no system)        a high finding
testing-procedure-2026-08-03-h1  [finding/unreviewed/high]  Testing procedure  a high finding
```

Every finding imported from this system's own audit docs is invisible to `tasks list --system "Task system"` and to the per-system views the carve-out was done to enable.

**Fix:** add `['task-system', 'Task system']` to `DOC_SYSTEM_PREFIXES`. Better, derive the map from `systems.json` (slugified names) so declaring a system cannot leave a second table stale — this is the "systems required to be manually kept in sync" shape CLAUDE.md forbids.

title: A [cN] tag is load-bearing identity but sits outside the deliverable freeze
deliverable: The freeze covers clause identity as well as clause prose, and duplicate or renumbered tags are refused by tasks check and the merge gate, not only by tasks audit. Today a prose-preserving tag edit is invisible to both.
evidence: In a scratch fixture, audit --proof 1=unmet --proof 2=met made the gate refuse with 'proof clause 1 is unmet as of pass 1'. Hand-editing that clause's tag from [c1] to [c2], prose untouched, made the line disappear: checkMergeGate walks clauses to verdicts and never verdicts to clauses, so a verdict whose clause id no longer exists is never read. tasks check reports 0 errors against a spec with two clauses tagged [c1]. Swapping [c1] and [c2] between two clauses passes check --merge with 0 issues while the recorded '- proof N:' lines now name different prose. The duplicate guard at tasks.ts:1164 is correctly sequenced within cmdAudit and is reached by the interactive walk, but it is the only place the invariant holds.

title: An undelivered task whose clause an amendment deletes can be neither done nor declined, and no command repoints it
deliverable: Dropping a proof clause through the sanctioned spec amend path leaves a closable task: either audit retires the undelivered task whose clause the amendment removed, or a command repoints it, so the branch is not left permanently unmergeable with hand-editing docs/tasks.jsonl as the only exit.
evidence: Sanctioned workflow only, no hand-editing: audit clause 1 unmet, delete the clause, spec amend, re-audit. done refuses with 'proof clause 1 is no longer in ...', decline refuses with 'undelivered and cannot be declined', and check --merge refuses forever on 'member(s) neither done nor declined'. The only exit is hand-editing docs/tasks.jsonl. Pre-existing on main, where clause-text matching deadlocked identically, so narrowed by this branch rather than introduced.
reason: We will only consider this once the event actually occurs.

title: New comments restate a test and describe other modules contracts
deliverable: The four comments added carry only facts their own file owns: the id-allocation rule lives in its test and in resolveIds, and the freezes rationale lives with the freeze in mergeGate.ts.
evidence: ProofClause.id's 'the lowest id no tag has claimed, in document order' is verbatim the name of its own test in specDoc.test.ts. stripClauseTags' comment explains the freeze's rationale from inside specDoc.ts, and Task.clause's comment describes the spec-file tag format from inside taskStore.ts - both describe another module's contract, which CLAUDE.md forbids. undeliveredDoneRefusal's tail and stampClauseIds' second sentence each restate a passing test. About 20 comment lines against about 55 new source lines.

title: stampClauseIds writes ids into nested sub-bullets, hardening a parse quirk into recorded identity
deliverable: Only a top-level bullet under Proof: is a clause, so an indented sub-point stays prose instead of being rewritten into the document with an id a verdict can name.
evidence: A '  - sub-point' indented under a clause is scanned as a clause of its own, because scanProofClauses matches '- ' against the trimmed line, and stampClauseIds then rewrites it into the document as '  - [c2] sub-point'. The mis-parse predates this branch; what is new is that the tool now writes the id into the human's document and lets a verdict name it. No spec under docs/specs/ currently uses a sub-bullet under Proof:, so nothing is mis-tagged today.

title: The first stamp can silently rebind verdicts recorded before tags existed
deliverable: A reader can tell which clause an old "- proof N:" line named: passes recorded under ordinal identity are either migrated when the spec is stamped or marked as predating the tags.
evidence: Simulated against a spec whose pass 1 recorded proof 1/2/3 under ordinal identity: deleting clause B before the first stamp leaves the survivors stamped [c1] [c2], so pass 1's '- proof 2: unmet - B did not hold' now sits beside a c2 that is old clause C. Inherited from ordinal identity rather than introduced, but stamping is the moment identity freezes and nothing marks which passes predate it. The real docs/specs/task-system-v2.md is unaffected: its clauses 7-8 were appended, not inserted.
reason: This type of bulletproofing is not necessary for the system at the moment.

title: A new clause inherits the met verdict of a deleted clause whose id it recycles
deliverable: An id retired by deleting its clause is never handed to a different clause, so a clause the deliverable gained after the last audit pass cannot reach the merge gate carrying a verdict recorded for something else.
evidence: Sanctioned path only, no hand-editing of the store or the pass record. Three clauses alpha/beta/gamma; tasks audit --proof 1=met 2=met 3=met stamps [c1][c2][c3]. Replace the [c2] beta line with an untagged bullet, then tasks spec amend to reset the freeze baseline. resolveIds hands the newcomer the lowest unclaimed id, which is the freed 2, so pass 1 proof 2: met now grades a clause no auditor has ever seen. tasks check --merge reports 0 issues with no new audit pass recorded. Both new gate walks pass because the id mapping is still a bijection, and duplicate detection sees nothing. specDoc.test.ts:57 asserts the opposite in its own name, so a new clause never steals an existing one, but only exercises an id a live neighbour holds, never one a graded clause retired.

title: docs/tasks.jsonl now serialises the same record in two different key orders
deliverable: Every line of the store carries the same field order whichever command wrote it, so a diff shows what changed rather than which code path touched the line.
evidence: loadStore spreads the parsed task then appends clause, so a task written before the field existed gets clause last while cmdAdd, cmdAudit and cmdImport place it after spec. Counted on the current store: 170 lines end with closed then clause, and 8 read spec then clause then requires. That split is most of the 349-line docs/tasks.jsonl diff this branch shows, and it will churn again whenever an old line is next rewritten.

title: evidence after a finding silently swallows clause evidence and overwrites the finding evidence
deliverable: A clause-shaped --evidence N=... typed after a --finding is either refused or routed to clause N, and a second --evidence on the same finding is refused rather than replacing the first, so nothing an auditor typed is dropped without a word.
evidence: Run in a temp fixture: tasks audit demo-spec --proof 1=met --proof 2=unmet --finding some-bug --severity low --system Runtime --deliverable fix-it --evidence broken-here --evidence 2=the-clause-did-not-hold. Exit 0, no warning. The spec records - proof 2: unmet with no evidence at all, the undelivered task demo-spec-clause-2 carries none, and the finding evidence reads literally 2=the-clause-did-not-hold, the auditor real evidence broken-here having been silently overwritten because the last --evidence wins. --file, the flag this positional overloading was copied from, appends instead of replacing, so the same keystroke loses nothing there.

title: handoff asserts a branch has no plan of its own when the trailer is only past the 20-commit cap
deliverable: The two ways the walk can come back empty are told apart: nothing on the branch at all, versus nothing within the commits scanned, so handoff never states as fact something it did not establish.
evidence: In a throwaway repo: a branch off main whose first commit carries Next: the branch plan, followed by 25 trailerless fixups. tasks handoff prints (no Next: trailer yet on this branch - nothing recorded since it left main), which is false; the branch does carry one, 26 commits back. Before e3b31a9 the same case printed the honest (no Next: trailer found in the last 20 commits), so the cap turned from a claim about the scan into a claim about the branch. Not hypothetical here: git rev-list --count puts the branch this one follows, task-system-v2, at 41 commits and archive/task-system-v1 at 24.

title: handoff walks unscoped when the base ref is missing, restoring the trailer it exists to suppress
deliverable: A merge-base that cannot be computed is distinguished from an empty range, so handoff says it could not find the branch point rather than falling back to the walk this branch removed.
evidence: branchCommitRange returns null for both cases. Measured two ways in throwaway repos: delete the local main after branching, or name the base trunk and leave the default --base-branch main. Both make tasks handoff print Next: OTHER BRANCH PLAN, the previous branch trailer, which is exactly the misdirection clause 5 forbids. A single-branch or shallow clone is the realistic shape; a depth-1 clone was also measured and falls to the same unscoped path. handoff is not run in CI, so the exposure is developer-local.

title: tasks check crashes on a directory named like a markdown file under docs/specs
deliverable: The per-push spec scan reads only regular files and survives one it cannot parse, so a stray path under docs/specs cannot take down the CI step that exists to validate the task store.
evidence: specIssues calls readFileSync on every readdirSync entry ending in .md without checking it is a file. mkdir docs/specs/archive.md then tasks check exits 1 with an unhandled EISDIR stack trace and prints no task-store result at all. Separately, a non-spec notes.md containing a Deliverable heading, a Proof: line and two [c1] bullets reddens tasks check repo-wide with error: notes tags more than one proof clause. Both measured in a temp specs dir. tasks check runs on every push on both matrix legs of .github/workflows/test.yml. Runtime is not the concern: the whole command is 267ms on the real repository.

title: the task CLI silently ignores unknown flags, so a planner's question returns a confident wrong answer
deliverable: an unrecognised flag on any command is an error naming the flag and the command's accepted flags; --help on any command or subcommand prints that command's usage and exits 0
evidence: Measured on task-system-policy-seam at 028507f. 'tasks list --blocked', 'tasks list --totallyfakeflag' and 'tasks list --help' each printed the full 87-task list with exit 0. 'tasks list --state bogus' IS rejected, so flag values are validated and flag names are not. Three commands answer --help three ways: list runs the query, spec prints usage, show errors. Why: the tool exists so a planner can ask what is blocked; 'list --blocked' answers that question with every task in the store and no indication it did not understand. How to apply: validate flag names in parseArgs against a per-command allowlist; route --help to usage. Re-measured at f0936dc and it is worse on a write than on a read: 'tasks edit pass2-c-m3 --state open' exits 0 and prints 'pass2-c-m3: nothing to change'. The flag is unknown, silently dropped, and the command then reports a confident no-op - so a caller who asked for a state change is told nothing changed, which is true and is not an answer to the question. cmdEdit builds its changes list from the flags it recognises and treats an empty list as success, so every unrecognised flag lands there. list at least returns data; edit returns a sentence that reads like a reason.

title: Unmet deliverable clause 1: `tasks next` and `tasks check` return in under a second against a 200-task store. The store this replaces cost 19s at 94 tasks and 30s at 105, and the growth driver was the audit protocol itself.
deliverable: `tasks next` and `tasks check` query a 200-task store in under 200ms, excluding interpreter startup. The store this replaces cost 19s at 94 tasks and 30s at 105, spending it on 94 file reads and a `git log --follow` called from inside a sort comparator.
evidence: npm run tasks -- next/check measured 1.1-1.6s wall time against a 200-task store; a no-op invocation alone costs ~1.3s (tsx transpile-on-every-run), the query logic itself adds only ~100-200ms. node --experimental-strip-types cuts the same call to ~0.15s but needs Node 22.6+, and test.yml pins node-version: 20 - not a same-session fix.

title: Split the task-system suite by command family
Shorten sentence-length task titles
deliverable: A single manual pass over kind=task records whose titles read as sentences, rewriting each to a four-or-five word summary. No hard limit is implemented and no validation is added. Ids unchanged. Findings keep their titles, since a finding title is the defect statement its audit filed.

title: tasks check reports freeze warnings for specs belonging to other branches
deliverable: check's spec warnings are scoped to the branch's own spec, or the report distinguishes this branch's specs from the rest of the store
evidence: Measured on task-system-policy-seam at 028507f. Every 'tasks check' and 'tasks check --merge' invocation on this branch emits three warnings about combat-continuation-runtime, task-system-small-test-fixes-to-get-feet-wet and task-system-v2 needing a freeze. None is this branch's work. Why: noise in the one command a planner runs to ask whether the branch is provable trains the reader to skip its output. Deletion by U2; doctor's report format is U3's.

title: tasks check stack-traces instead of reporting on a conflicted or malformed store
deliverable: loadStore reports a parse or shape failure as a check error naming the file and line number, instead of throwing an uncaught SyntaxError or TypeError.
evidence: loadStore does a bare JSON.parse per line with no line number, file name or shape validation. A store carrying git conflict markers dies with SyntaxError; a row missing requires dies with TypeError from inside checkStore. The design sells JSONL on merging clean, so the unclean case is the one that needs a readable failure, and it lands on the CI step named check.

title: tasks plan now exits 1 on a malformed systems.json, and it is an unguarded CI step

title: a blocked deferred finding is counted in the header but appears in no footer row, so the roadmap's 'nothing is hidden' promise has a hole

title: roadmap.ts and roadmapCmd.ts both describe tasks next's contract in a comment, which CLAUDE.md forbids
deliverable: CLAUDE.md's comment policy says never describe another module's contract, because that comment drifts the moment its owner changes and the owner is the ground truth a reader should go to. roadmap.ts:49-51 states that tasks next 'deliberately refuses to read a null spec as this query', and roadmapCmd.ts:90-92 restates it. title: roadmapCmd re-implements render.ts's greedy wrap and its ellipsis truncation, and re-declares the 78 both are measured against
deliverable: One truncation rule and one greedy-pack rule in scripts/tasks/, reached by both renderers, and one declaration of the 78-column terminal width. Today there are two of each, in sibling files of the same layer — the class of hand-synchronised duplicate CLAUDE.md's mission names outright.
evidence: roadmapCmd.ts:16 is 'text.length > width ? text.slice(0, width - 1) + ellipsis : text.padEnd(width)'; render.ts:125 truncateLine is 'text.length > max ? text.slice(0, max - 1) + ellipsis : text' — the same expression, differing only in the pad, so fit could be truncateLine(text, width).padEnd(width). roadmapCmd.ts:84 packed() and render.ts:107 wrapText() are the same greedy accumulator loop line for line — the candidate variable, the 'candidate.length > width && current !== 0-length' flush, the trailing push — differing only in joining an array with a separator instead of splitting a string on spaces. roadmapCmd.ts:5 declares WIDTH = 78 while render.ts:102 declares EVIDENCE_WRAP_WIDTH = 78 - indent; the branch's own spec (Decisions, 'Fixed width, truncating') says the width was chosen 'matching EVIDENCE_WRAP_WIDTH in render.ts' — a match by copying the literal, not by reference, so changing one leaves the other silently wrong. title: the commit that closed the forbidden-comment finding added two more comments of the same class
deliverable: The two new source files carry only comments that pass CLAUDE.md's test — owned by the file, not derivable from reading it, and expressible as neither a name, a type nor a test. Each block below fails that test with a named passing test to point at instead, so deleting it loses nothing and git holds every word.

A comment restating a finding is a third copy that cannot be executed and will rot.' title: the gui-rebuild title rewrite dropped 'designed for mobile', a constraint the record holds nowhere else
deliverable: gui-rebuild's evidence carries the mobile-first constraint again, so c8's rule holds for every rewritten record: a shortened title may only drop a fact the record still holds. title: `comment-only` certifies commits that deleted CI steps, disabled tests, and neutered gates
evidence:
**Verified against four throwaway commits.** CLAUDE.md:19 states the contract:

> Strip passes must pass `npm run comment-only -- <base>`, which **proves no code changed**.

It proves something much narrower. `comment-only-diff.ts:5` sets
`SOURCE_EXTENSIONS = ['.ts', '.tsx']`, and `:38` skips every other path outright:

```ts
if (!SOURCE_EXTENSIONS.some((extension) => path.endsWith(extension))) continue;
```

A single commit that stripped comments from `src/runtime/tuning.ts` **and**, in the same commit:

- deleted `- run: npm test` and `- run: npm run audit-status` from `.github/workflows/test.yml`,
- renamed `# test tutorial-quest-given` to `# test DISABLED-…` in the shipped content,
- replaced `"comment-budget": "tsx scripts/comment-ratio.ts"` with `"comment-budget": "echo skip"`,

reports:

```
<base>..HEAD is comment-only: 1 files changed, all code identical after stripping comments.
```

exit 0. Three narrower probes isolate the mechanism:

| Fixture | Reported | Actual |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strip + gut CI + disable a `# test` + neuter `comment-budget` | `is comment-only` | four files changed |
| Change **only** `test.yml` (`comment-budget` → `true`) | `is comment-only: **0 files changed**` | one file changed |
| `--worktree` + a new **untracked** `src/runtime/sneaky.ts` | `is comment-only` | a new source file appeared |
| Intra-line whitespace (`export function` → `export  function`) | correctly **fails** | — |

The second row is the cleanest statement of the defect: the tool prints "0 files changed" about a
commit that changed a file, because the file was not a `.ts`. The third is worse in one way —
`git diff` never lists untracked paths, so `--worktree` mode cannot see an added file at all,
while the tracked-file path at `:40` explicitly rejects additions with "a comment-only change adds
no files".

The blast radius is specific to this system: the set of files `comment-only` cannot see is almost
exactly the set that defines whether this repo's gates run at all — `test.yml`, `package.json`'s
script bodies, and `content/*.dsl`. A strip pass is the one commit shape reviewers are encouraged
to skim, and it is the shape this gate is supposed to make safe to skim.

Note the same repo already computes this correctly elsewhere: `audit-status.ts:51-59` handles
non-TypeScript files by comparing them **verbatim**, with a comment explaining exactly why. Two
scripts sharing `codeOnly` reached opposite conclusions about the same problem.

**Fix**: mirror `audit-status`'s `STRIPPABLE` split — compare non-`.ts` paths byte-for-byte and
diverge on any difference, rather than `continue`. Additionally, in `--worktree` mode, list
untracked files (`git ls-files --others --exclude-standard`) and treat any source addition as a
divergence, matching the tracked-path rule at `:40`.
reason: Dead: comment-only and the comment gates it certified were retired 2026-07-28 per CLAUDE.md.

title: the shipped `# test` corpus is two happy paths, and never uses its strongest assertion
evidence:
**Measured by mutation testing.** The corpus is two sections in `content/tutorial-island.dsl`:
`tutorial-quest-given` (4 lines) and `miki-route-full` (~25 lines). Seven single-token mutants,
run against the corpus in isolation and against the full suite:

| Mutant | 2 shipped `# test`s | `npm test` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `conditions.ts`: `>=` → `>` | caught | caught (7 failed) |
| `conditions.ts`: `not` stops negating | caught | caught (8 failed) |

| `effects.ts`: resource max-clamp inverted | **SURVIVES** | caught (12 failed) |

4 of 6 — meaningfully better than "replays a happy path", and worth saying plainly, since the

title: the "an audit doc is required" gate is satisfiable by `touch`
evidence:
**Verified.** CLAUDE.md:31 makes the doc load-bearing:

> The doc is required — a counter reset with nothing to show for it fails the same check.

`audit-status.ts:82-84` implements that as an existence test and nothing more:

```ts
function documented(system: System): boolean {
  return system.lastAudit === null || (system.lastAuditDoc !== null && existsSync(system.lastAuditDoc));
}
```

Setting `lastAuditDoc` to each of the following, with `lastAudit: "83d81d2"`:

| `lastAuditDoc` value | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `docs/audits` (a **directory**) | passes, exit 0 |
| `package.json` (an unrelated tracked file) | passes, exit 0 |
| `docs/audits/empty-audit.md` (**zero bytes**) | passes, exit 0 |

The check cannot tell an audit from an empty file, does not require the path to be under
`docs/audits/`, does not require it to be a file at all, and never relates the document to the
`lastAudit` SHA it is meant to evidence. Since this is the mechanism that turns CI red until an
audit lands, the cheapest way to make CI green is `touch docs/audits/x.md` — which is precisely
the failure mode the sentence in CLAUDE.md was written to prevent, and which the current
`systems.json` history shows already happened once (three markers recorded `83d81d2` with no doc,
reset in `f16ccb1`).

**Fix**: require `lastAuditDoc` to match `^docs/audits/.+\.md$`, to be a regular file
(`statSync().isFile()`), to be non-trivially sized, and — the part that actually binds the doc to
the claim — to contain the `lastAudit` short SHA. Each is one line and together they make the
marker unforgeable without writing something.

title: the commit hook fires on strings that merely contain "git commit", and stays silent on the commands that most need it
evidence:
**Verified by feeding `.claude/hooks/audit-due.sh` synthetic PostToolUse payloads.**
`audit-due.sh:5-8` dispatches on an unanchored glob over the raw command text:

```bash
case "$command" in
  *git\ commit*) ;;
  *) exit 0 ;;
esac
```

| Tool command | Hook fires | Should it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `git commit -m x` | **yes** | yes |
| `git status` | no | no |
| `echo "git commit"` | **yes** | no |
| `git log --grep="git commit"` | **yes** | no |
| `git commit --dry-run` | **yes** | no — nothing was committed |
| `git merge feature` | **no** | yes — HEAD moved, budgets can cross the threshold |
| `git rebase main` | **no** | yes — same |
| malformed stdin / `node` missing | no (exit 0) | fail-open, silently disabled |

Three separate problems, all verified:

1. **False positives.** Any command whose text contains the substring triggers a full
   `audit-status` run and an `exit 2` blocking error. `--dry-run` is the sharpest case: the hook
   announces "The git command above ran normally" about a command that deliberately committed
   nothing.
2. **False negatives.** `git merge` and `git rebase` both move HEAD and can push a system past the
   threshold; neither matches. The signal advertised as firing "on commit" has holes in both
   directions.
3. **The message asserts two facts it never checks.** `audit-due.sh:17` says *"The git command
   above ran normally"* and *"reporting on the new HEAD"*. The hook reads only
   `tool_input.command` (via `tool-command.js`), never the tool's exit status — so a **failed**
   commit produces the same "ran normally". And it runs `npm run audit-status` in the hook's own
   cwd, which I confirmed is the project root regardless of a `cd` in the command: committing
   inside a worktree (`cd /some/worktree && git commit`) reports on the **main** repo's HEAD while
   claiming to report on "the new HEAD". I hit this live — every commit I made in the audit
   worktree produced a report about the main tree.

None of this can wedge the repo: it is a PostToolUse hook, so the commit has already happened and
`exit 2` only feeds text back to the agent. That is worth stating explicitly, because "gates
commits" in the commit subject (`0699072`, "Make the audit signal fire on commit and gate CI")
overstates it — CI is the gate; the hook is a notification.

**Fix**: match on the command's leading token rather than a substring (or parse `git\s+commit\b`
with a negative lookahead for `--dry-run`), add `git merge` and `git rebase` to the trigger, read
the tool result to confirm success before claiming it, and either run `audit-status` in the
command's working directory or drop "the new HEAD" from the message.
reason: Closed per testing-procedure-2026-07-30.md's intro ("closed in completed-tasks.md").

**Verified two ways.** `runTest` has no vocabulary for modals. Replaying the shipped

```ts

```

so the modal it leaves behind lands in the REPL. Piping

```
[time: 107.2s]
Name: Race:
  1) Human  2) Elf  3) Dwarf  4) Orc

```

The modal consumed `/test miki-route-full` as the player's **name** and `/quit` as the **race**.

**Overlaps a tracked item — merge, do not double-count.** `backlog.md` already tracks
